cases.title: Union of India v. The Algorithm Audit Board
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Parliament of India passed the "National Security (Digital
Surveillance) Act." Section 12 of this parent Act empowered the Ministry
of Home Affairs (MHA) to "frame rules and deploy technological tools to
identify and neutralize digital threats to the sovereignty of India."
Under this broad delegation, the MHA notified the "AI Surveillance
Rules, 2026." These rules authorized the deployment of an autonomous AI
system, "Sovereign-Sentinel," which possessed the power to flag "anti-
national" social media accounts and automatically suspend them without
prior notice. Crucially, the rules did not define "anti-national,"
leaving the AI to develop its own evolving criteria based on "deep
learning." The Algorithm Audit Board, an independent NGO, filed a writ
petition in the Supreme Court, arguing that Section 12 suffered from
"Excessive Delegation" and that the 2026 Rules were ultra vires
(beyond the powers of) the parent Act because the MHA had abdicated its
"Essential Legislative Function" to an algorithm.
cases.issues:
- Does Section 12 of the Digital Surveillance Act constitute an
unconstitutional abdication of "Essential Legislative Functions" by the
Parliament?
- Can a parent Act delegate the power to define "legal standards" (such
as what constitutes a threat) to an executive-controlled AI?
Are the 2026 Rules ultra vires on the grounds of "Unreasonableness"
and "Manifest Arbitrariness"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Audit Board)
The Petitioners relied on the landmark judgment in In re Delhi Laws Act
and A.N. Parasuraman v. State of Tamil Nadu. They argued that the
legislature must lay down a "clear policy or standard." Section 12 is a
"blank check," providing no guidance or boundaries. They contended that
defining the "substance" of what is a crime or a threat is an Essential
Legislative Function that cannot be delegated. By allowing an AI to
define "anti-national," the Parliament had essentially allowed a machine
to write the law, violating the Separation of Powers.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that in the modern digital era, the legislature
cannot foresee every dynamic threat. Relying on Avinder Singh v. State
of Punjab, they argued that "administrative pragmatism" requires broad
delegation. They contended that Section 12 provided a sufficient "policy
guide" (sovereignty and integrity of India). The State argued that the AI
was merely a "technical tool" for execution, not a legislator, and that
judicial review of the AI's logic was sufficient protection.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Algorithm Audit Board. The Court
struck down the 2026 Rules as unconstitutional and held Section 12 to be
partially void for Excessive Delegation. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Administrative
Accountability. The judge ruled that the legislature cannot delegate
"naked and uncanalized power." While "procedural" details can be
delegated, the "policy" must be defined by the elected representatives.
The Court reasoned that "Delegated legislation is a child of the parent
Act; a child cannot be more powerful than the parent."

The judge held that delegating the power to define a "standard of
conduct" to an AI-whose logic is opaque-is a total abdication of
legislative duty. The Court applied the Doctrine of Non-Delegability of
Essential Functions, ruling that identifying what speech is "anti-
national" is a value-based human legal judgment, not a mathematical
execution. Allowing a machine to create its own standards of censorship
destroys the Rule of Law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Algorithmic Delegation. It
reinforces that Essential Legislative Functions (policy making) cannot
be delegated to the Executive or AI, and that any delegated legislation
must have "intelligible guidelines" within the parent Act to survive the
test of Article 14.

cases.title: Dr. Neha v. State Medical Council
cases.facts:
Dr. Neha, a senior surgeon, was summarily suspended by the State Medical
Council following a single anonymous complaint regarding "unethical
practices." The Council invoked its "Emergency Disciplinary Power" under
Regulation 45, which allowed for immediate suspension "to protect the
public interest" without a prior hearing. No show-cause notice was
issued. After the suspension, Dr. Neha's clinic was sealed. The Council
offered her a "reconsideration hearing" thirty days after the suspension.
Dr. Neha challenged the suspension in the High Court, arguing that the
failure to provide a "Pre-Decisional Hearing" violated the Principles
of Natural Justice (Audi Alteram Partem).
cases.issues:
- Is the "Pre-Decisional Hearing" an absolute requirement of
Administrative Law, or can it be dispensed with in "exceptional
circumstances"?
- Can a "Post-Decisional Hearing" cure a procedural defect if the initial
action was taken without notice?
- Does the seal of a clinic and suspension of a professional license
without a hearing constitute "civil death"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Dr. Neha)
The Petitioner relied on Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India and Ridge v.
Baldwin. She argued that the right to be heard is an "immutable" part of
the Rule of Law. Suspension of a medical license is a "civil death" that
destroys reputation and livelihood. She contended that "Emergency" is
often used as a cloak for administrative high-handedness. A post-
decisional hearing is an "empty formality" because the Council has
already formed a biased opinion by taking the action.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Medical Council)
The Council argued that the "Public Interest" necessitated immediate
action to prevent further harm to patients. Relying on Swadeshi Cotton
Mills v. Union of India, they argued that when "urgent action" is
required, the requirements of natural justice can be tailored. They
contended that since a hearing was offered thirty days later, the Dr.
Neha's right to be heard was preserved, just "delayed."
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Dr. Neha. The suspension was quashed for
violating the fundamental principles of natural justice. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a profound judgment on Procedural Fairness. The
judge ruled that the "audi alteram partem" rule is not a "meaningless
ritual" but a constitutional mandate.

The judge reasoned that a Post-Decisional Hearing is generally not an
acceptable substitute for a Pre-Decisional Hearing, especially when the
action taken is irreversible or carries a heavy social stigma. The Court
noted that unless the State can prove an "immediate and catastrophic
threat to life," the Council must provide at least a "summary hearing" or
a 24-hour show-cause notice. The judge held that the seal of the clinic
without even a prima facie inquiry was "manifestly arbitrary." The
Council's "emergency" rationale was deemed a "perverse exercise of power"
that bypassed Dr. Neha's fundamental right to dignity.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Primacy of Pre-Decisional Hearings. It
establishes that the "Public Interest" exception must be interpreted
narrowly, and that a post-decisional hearing can only cure a defect if
the initial action was truly urgent and the subsequent hearing is a
genuine, unbiased "de novo" consideration.

cases.title: Apex Infra v. The Tender Committee
cases.facts:
The State Government issued a global tender for a ₹5,000 Crore highway
project. The tender document specified that "the lowest bidder (L1) with
a 10-year experience record shall be awarded the contract." Apex Infra
was the L1 bidder and met all criteria. However, after the bids were
opened, the Tender Committee changed the criteria to "Green-Tech
certification," a requirement not mentioned in the original tender. They
then awarded the contract to a rival, "Eco-Build," who was the L3 bidder
but had the certification. Apex Infra challenged the decision, citing
"Legitimate Expectation" and "Procedural Impropriety."
cases.issues:
- Can the State change the "rules of the game" after the "game" (tender
process) has already started?
- Does a bidder have a "Legitimate Expectation" to be treated according
to the criteria published in the initial tender?
- What is the scope of Judicial Review over the
commercial/contractual decisions of the State?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Apex Infra)
The Petitioner relied on Food Corporation of India v. Kamdhenu Cattle
Feed Industries. They argued that the State must act fairly and non-
arbitrarily even in commercial matters. By changing the rules mid-way to
favor a specific bidder (Eco-Build), the Committee acted with mala
fides. They argued that "Legitimate Expectation" is a facet of Article
14; once the State invites bids on certain terms, it is "estopped" from
introducing new conditions at the stage of evaluation.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State)
The State argued that as the "consumer," it has the absolute right to
choose the best technology. They contended that "Green-Tech" was
essential for the environmental goals of the State (Directive
Principles). Relying on Tata Cellular v. Union of India, they argued
that the Court should not sit as an "appellate body" over technical
tender decisions and that "Legitimate Expectation" cannot override the
"Public Interest."
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Apex Infra. The Court quashed the
award to Eco-Build and ordered a fresh tender process. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Administrative Transparency. The
judge applied the Wednesbury Principles of Reasonableness. The Court
ruled that while the State has "commercial freedom," it cannot be
"capricious."

The reasoning was that "the State must play fair." Introducing a new
criterion after the bids are opened is the "hallmark of arbitrariness."
The judge held that Apex Infra had a Legitimate Expectation to be
evaluated based on the criteria they relied upon when spending millions
to prepare the bid. The Court reasoned that if the State wanted Green-
Tech, it should have stated so in the original document. Changing the
rules mid-way is a "procedural impropriety" that violates Article 14. The
"Public Interest" in green technology does not grant the State a license
to violate the Rule of Law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Fairness in Tenders. It
reinforces that Legitimate Expectation is an enforceable right in
Administrative Law and that judicial review extends to commercial
actions of the State to prevent "favoritism and mid-stream changes."

cases.title: Union of India v. The Tribunal Reforms Union
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Parliament passed the "Tribunal Efficiency Act," which gave
the Central Government the power to appoint and remove members of various
tribunals (like the NGT and NCLT) through an executive committee, without
the involvement of the Judiciary. The Act also mandated that the
"Selection Committee" would be dominated by government secretaries. The
Tribunal Reforms Union filed a writ petition, arguing that the Act
destroyed the Independence of the Judiciary and converted tribunals
into "puppets of the executive."
cases.issues:
- Are Tribunals "courts" for the purpose of the Separation of Powers?
- Does executive control over the appointment and tenure of tribunal
members violate the Basic Structure of the Constitution?
- Can a quasi-judicial body function effectively if its members are
dependent on the government for their livelihood?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Union)
The Petitioners relied on L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India and R.
Gandhi v. Union of India. They argued that tribunals perform "judicial
functions" and are substitutes for the High Courts. Therefore, they must
have the same "insulation" from the executive. They contended that if the
government is the largest litigator (which it is), allowing the
government to choose the judges who will hear those cases is a violation
of the maxim Nemo judex in causa sua (No one should be a judge in their
own cause).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that Tribunals are "specialized bodies" meant for
efficiency, not "subordinate courts." They contended that Article 323A
and 323B give the Parliament plenary power to create and regulate
tribunals. They argued that executive involvement ensures "administrative
speed" and that the judiciary has no constitutional right to manage the
appointment of quasi-judicial experts.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Reforms Union. The Court struck
down the Act's appointment provisions as unconstitutional. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a definitive ruling on the Independence of
Tribunals. The judge ruled that Tribunals are part of the "Justice
Delivery System." The judge reasoned that any body performing a
"Judicial Function" must be independent of the executive. To have a
Selection Committee dominated by bureaucrats-when the government is a
party in 90% of the cases-is a "Structural Bias" that destroys the
public's faith in the law. The Court held that Judicial Independence
is a part of the Basic Structure and it extends to Tribunals. The
Court mandated that the Selection Committee must be headed by the Chief
Justice of India or a nominee to ensure "judicial oversight" of quasi-
judicial appointments.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Judicial Independence in
Tribunals. It establishes that Tribunals must be "insulated" from
executive influence to maintain the Separation of Powers, and that the
judiciary must have a "meaningful voice" in the selection of tribunal
members.

cases.title: State of Vindhya v. The Civil Service Association
cases.facts:
The State Government of Vindhya issued an order of "Compulsory
Retirement" against ten senior civil servants, including a highly
decorated officer, Mr. Rajat, citing "loss of utility" and "dead wood."
The order was based on the "Subjective Satisfaction" of a Review
Committee. However, Mr. Rajat's recent Annual Confidential Reports (ACRs)
were all marked "Outstanding." The State argued that ACRs are not the
only metric and that they possessed the absolute "Pleasure Power" to
retire officers in the public interest. Rajat challenged the order as
"Malicious and Perverse."
cases.issues:
- Is the "Subjective Satisfaction" of the State in matters of compulsory
retirement immune from Judicial Review?
- Can the State retire an officer as "dead wood" if their recent
performance records are "Outstanding"?
- Does compulsory retirement based on no material evidence constitute a
"Penalty" without a trial?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Rajat)
The Petitioner relied on Baikuntha Nath Das v. Chief District Medical
Officer. He argued that "Subjective Satisfaction" is not "Absolute
Satisfaction." The State must have some "material" on record to justify
the decision. He contended that ignoring his "Outstanding" ACRs proved
that the decision was not based on "performance" but on "personal
vendetta," making it Mala Fide.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State)
The State argued that compulsory retirement is not a "punishment" but an
"administrative housekeeping" measure. They contended that under
Fundamental Rule 56(j), the State has a "Sovereign Discretion" to retire
officers. They argued that the "satisfaction" is purely internal and that
the Court cannot substitute its own opinion for that of the Review
Committee.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Mr. Rajat. The Court quashed the
compulsory retirement order. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on the Limits of Discretionary Power.
The judge ruled that "Subjective Satisfaction" must be based on
"Objective Material."

The judge reasoned that while the Court will not judge the sufficiency
of the material, it will certainly judge the existence of it. Ignoring
the most recent "Outstanding" records and relying on ancient or non-
existent data makes the decision Perverse. The Court held that
compulsory retirement cannot be used as a "short-cut" to bypass
disciplinary proceedings for alleged misconduct. The judge famously
remarked, "Discretion is not a license for whim." If the records show the
officer is efficient, the label of "dead wood" is a "colorable exercise
of power" that violates Article 14.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Judicial Review of Subjective Satisfaction.
It establishes that administrative discretion must be exercised on
"relevant material," and that ignoring positive records makes an
administrative action "arbitrary and mala fide."

cases.title: The Coastal Residents v. The Environmental Clearance Board
cases.facts:
The Environmental Clearance Board granted a massive clearance for a
thermal power plant project on the coast of Karnataka. It was later
discovered that the Chairman of the Board held 10,000 shares in the
company that was building the power plant. The Coastal Residents
challenged the clearance, alleging "Pecuniary Bias." The Chairman
argued that 10,000 shares were "negligible" in a multi-billion dollar
company and that he had no actual influence over the technical experts
who drafted the report.
cases.issues:
- Does the "existence" of a pecuniary (financial) interest automatically
disqualify an administrative decision-maker, or must "actual bias" be
proven?
- Does the Doctrine of Necessity allow a biased official to
participate if no other authority is available?
- What is the threshold for the "Real Likelihood of Bias" test in
Administrative Law?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Residents)
The Petitioners relied on the ancient maxim Nemo debet esse judex in
propria causa. They argued that in the case of Pecuniary Bias, even
the "slightest interest" is sufficient to invalidate the decision.
Relying on Dimes v. Grand Junction Canal, they argued that "Justice
must not only be done, but must be seen to be done." The public cannot
trust a clearance signed by a man who stands to profit, however small the
amount.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Board/Company)
The Company argued the "De Minimis" rule-that the interest was too small
to affect the Chairman's mind. They contended that the Board's decision
was a "collective act" of 20 experts and the Chairman was merely the
presiding officer. They argued that stopping a multi-crore project over a
few shares would lead to "litigious harassment" of officials.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Residents. The environmental
clearance was quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a strict ruling on Administrative Integrity. The
judge ruled that the rule against Pecuniary Bias is "Absolute and
Unqualified."

The judge reasoned that unlike "personal bias" (where a "real likelihood"
must be shown), "pecuniary bias" does not require proof of actual
influence. The very presence of a financial stake, no matter how small,
"poisons the fountain of justice." The judge held that "The law does not
measure the size of the interest, it only detects its presence." The
Court reasoned that to maintain the "Rule of Law," administrative bodies
must be above suspicion. The Chairman's participation rendered the entire
proceeding void ab initio.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Strict Liability Rule for Pecuniary Bias. It
establishes that any financial interest in the subject matter of a
dispute disqualifies a decision-maker, regardless of whether actual
bias influenced the outcome.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Heritage Restoration Society
cases.facts:
The State Government issued an administrative order to demolish a 150-
year-old historic clock tower to widen a road by only two meters. The
Heritage Society provided three alternative engineering plans that would
widen the road without touching the tower, though they were 10% more
expensive. The Government rejected the alternatives, stating they had
"unfettered administrative discretion" over urban planning. The Society
challenged the order as "Disproportionate and Unreasonable."
cases.issues:
- Is the "Wednesbury Principle" (where the Court only intervenes if the
decision is "so absurd that no reasonable person could make it") still
the only standard for reviewing administrative discretion?
- Can the Court apply the "Doctrine of Proportionality" to review the
merits of a policy decision involving infrastructure?
- Does the State have a duty to choose the "Least Restrictive Measure"
when public heritage is at stake?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Society)
The Petitioner relied on Om Kumar v. Union of India. They argued that
the Court must move from the "secondary review" of Wednesbury to the
"primary review" of Proportionality. They contended that the "End"
(widening the road) did not justify the "Means" (destroying a unique
heritage site) when a less-harmful alternative existed. They argued the
decision was "irrational" because the benefit (2 meters of road) was
negligible compared to the loss of history.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that they are the sole judges of "Public Utility."
They contended that applying "Proportionality" would allow judges to
become "Super-Architects," which violates the Separation of Powers. They
argued the decision met the "Wednesbury Test" because it was a "possible"
decision made by a legitimate authority.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Heritage Society. The demolition
order was quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark judgment on Substantive Review. The
judge ruled that for decisions affecting "Fundamental Interests" (like
heritage and environment), the Proportionality Test is the correct
standard.

The judge reasoned that the State must show that (1) the aim was
legitimate, (2) the measure was suitable, and (3) it was Necessary
(i.e., the least restrictive means was chosen). Since a viable
alternative existed that preserved the tower for only a marginal cost
increase, the State's choice to destroy the tower was "Disproportionate."
The Court held that Administrative Discretion is no longer a "Black Box"
into which the judiciary cannot look. "Reasonableness" now requires the
State to balance the competing interests fairly.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Primacy of the Proportionality Test over
the Wednesbury Principle in matters affecting significant public assets.
It reinforces the principle that the State must choose the "Least
Restrictive Measure" when exercising its discretionary powers.

cases.title: MegaLogistics v. The Port Authority
cases.facts:
The Port Authority verbally promised MegaLogistics that if they built a
private cold-storage facility on the port lands, the Authority would
grant them a 50% discount on berthing fees for 20 years. Relying on this
promise, MegaLogistics invested ₹200 Crores in the facility. Two years
later, the Authority issued a circular withdrawing all discounts, citing
"policy changes." MegaLogistics sued, invoking "Equitable Estoppel."
The Authority argued that "Estoppel" cannot be used against the State or
to bind future policy.
cases.issues:
- Can the "Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel" be invoked against a
statutory authority or the State?
- Does a "Change in Policy" provide a valid defense for the State to
renege on a specific commercial promise?
- Can the State claim "Sovereign Immunity" from its own contractual-style
representations?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (MegaLogistics)
The Petitioner relied on Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of UP.
They argued that the State is not "above the law." If a citizen alters
their position to their detriment based on a clear promise by the State,
the State must honor it. They contended that "Fairness" is the heart of
Administrative Law and that the State cannot act like a "deceptive
private trader."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Port Authority)
The Authority argued that they have a duty to maximize revenue for the
public exchequer. They contended that an "administrative promise" cannot
"freeze" the sovereign power to change tax or fee structures. Relying on
Kasinka Trading v. Union of India, they argued that "Public Interest"
in increasing port revenue must override the "Private Interest" of
MegaLogistics.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of MegaLogistics. The Court ordered the
Authority to honor the discount for the promised period. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a strong defense of State Accountability. The
judge ruled that Promissory Estoppel is a sword against
arbitrariness. The judge reasoned that the "Public Interest" defense is
not a "magic word" that wipes away all obligations. To defeat Estoppel,
the State must show a "Compelling and Supervening Public Interest" (like
a war or economic collapse) that makes it highly inequitable to hold
them to the promise. A mere desire to "make more money" or a "change in
policy" is not enough. The Court held that the credibility of the State
is a "Public Interest" in itself. If citizens cannot trust the State's
word, the entire economic fabric of the nation collapses.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel against the
State. It establishes that the Government is bound by its promises if
a citizen has acted upon them to their detriment, and the "Public
Interest" defense must meet a "high threshold of necessity" to be valid.

cases.title: The Citizen v. The Lokpal
cases.facts:
A citizen filed a detailed corruption complaint against a high-ranking
bureaucrat with the Lokpal (the anti-corruption ombudsman). The Lokpal
issued a one-line order: "Dismissed. No prima facie case found." The
Lokpal argued that under its parent Act, its "Satisfaction" was final and
it was not a "court," thus not required to give reasons. The citizen
filed a writ of Certiorari and Mandamus, demanding a "Reasoned
Order."
cases.issues:
- Is a quasi-judicial body like the Lokpal required to provide "Speaking
Orders" (Reasoned Decisions)?
- Can a "Negative Decision" (refusal to investigate) be subject to
Judicial Review?
- Does the "Right to Reason" form a part of the Principles of Natural
Justice in Administrative Law?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (The Citizen)
The Petitioner relied on S.N. Mukherjee v. Union of India. He argued
that "Reason is the heartbeat of a decision." Without reasons, a decision
is "blind" and judicial review is "crippled." He contended that an
ombudsman must be "transparent" to be "effective." A one-line dismissal
is the "hallmark of a star-chamber," not a democratic institution.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Lokpal)
The Lokpal argued that providing reasons in corruption cases could tip
off the accused or harm the "confidentiality" of its processes. They
contended that the statute granted them "Absolute Discretion" to decide
whether to proceed and that they were not "bound" by the strict rules of
civil courts.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Citizen. The Court quashed the one-
line order and issued a Mandamus to the Lokpal to pass a "Speaking
Order." The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Administrative Transparency. The
judge ruled that the "Duty to give Reasons" is the Third Principle
of Natural Justice.

The judge reasoned that "Reasons are the link between the mind of the
decision-maker and the actual controversy." Without reasons, the High
Court cannot know if the Lokpal applied its mind or acted out of
"political pressure." The Court held that confidentiality can be
maintained through "sealed covers," but the "substance of the reasoning"
must be communicated to the complainant. A "Reasonless Order" is ipso
facto arbitrary and violates Article 14. The judge noted that the more
powerful the authority, the more rigorous the duty to explain its
actions.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Mandatory Requirement of Speaking Orders.
It reinforces the principle that all quasi-judicial bodies must provide
reasons for their decisions, as the "Right to Reason" is an essential
safeguard against administrative arbitrariness.

cases.title: Tech-Flow v. The Data Protection Authority
cases.facts:
The "Data Protection Act, 2026" contained a "Finality Clause" (Section
99) which stated: "Every decision of the Data Protection Authority
regarding fines shall be final and shall not be called into question in
any court of law by way of appeal or otherwise." The Authority imposed a
₹100 Crore fine on Tech-Flow. Tech-Flow challenged the fine in the High
Court, alleging a "Jurisdictional Error." The Authority argued that
the High Court's jurisdiction was "Ousted" by the Finality Clause.
cases.issues:
- Can a "Finality Clause" in a statute "Oust" the constitutional power of
Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226?
- Does the Basic Structure Doctrine prevent Parliament from making an
administrative authority "un-challengeable"?
- What is the difference between a "statutory right of appeal" and
"constitutional judicial review"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Tech-Flow)
The Petitioner relied on L. Chandra Kumar and Minerva Mills. They
argued that Judicial Review is an un-amendable feature of the Basic
Structure. A "Finality Clause" can take away a "Statutory Appeal," but
it can never take away the High Court's power to issue writs. They
contended that if the Authority makes a "Jurisdictional Error" (acting
beyond its power), the High Court must intervene to maintain the Rule
of Law.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Authority)
The Authority argued for "Legislative Intent." They contended that the
data economy requires "certainty and speed." If every fine is tied up in
court for ten years, the Act becomes a "Dead Letter." They argued that
Parliament had the right to choose "Expert Finality" over "Judicial
Delay."
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Tech-Flow. The Court held that Section
99 could not block a Writ Petition. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a firm ruling on Constitutional Supremacy. [Image
showing the relationship between Judiciary, Legislature and Executive in
India] The judge ruled that the Parliament is a "creature of the
Constitution" and cannot destroy the "Check and Balance" system.

The judge reasoned that a "Finality Clause" is like a "Stay-Out" sign,
but the High Court possesses a "Constitutional Master-Key." The Court
held that even if a statute says an order is "Final," the Court can
always review the order on three grounds: (1) Lack of Jurisdiction,
(2) Violation of Natural Justice, and (3) Error of Law apparent on
the face of the record. The judge famously remarked, "Parliament can
make an authority 'final' in fact, but only the Constitution makes it
'final' in law." The "Ouster Clause" was read down to allow writ
jurisdiction.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Inalienability of Judicial
Review. It establishes the legal principle that no Act of Parliament
can take away the Writ Jurisdiction of the High Courts or the Supreme
Court, ensuring that every administrative authority remains "under the
law" and not "above it."

cases.title: Union of India v. CAPF Officers Association, 2026
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Supreme Court delivered a historic judgment (2025 INSC 779)
granting "Organised Group-A Service" (OGAS) status to all five Central
Armed Police Forces (CAPFs). This mandated that 50% of high-ranking posts
previously reserved for IPS officers on deputation be opened for internal
promotion of CAPF cadre officers. In early 2026, the Union Cabinet
introduced the "CAPF (General Administration & Regulation) Bill, 2026."
Section 4 of this Bill explicitly sought to revert the promotion
architecture to the pre-2025 status, effectively nullifying the Supreme
Court's operative directions under the guise of "national security
exigencies." The CAPF Officers Association challenged the Bill's approval
and introduction as a blatant violation of the Separation of Powers.
cases.issues:
Can the Legislature pass a law specifically to nullify the effect of a
binding judicial decree between the same parties?

Does the CAPF Bill, 2026, violate the Basic Structure by abrogating the
power of Judicial Review?

What is the threshold for a "validating law" to overcome a judicial
ruling without being classified as an "impermissible legislative
override"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Officers Association)
The Petitioners relied on L. Chandra Kumar and S.R. Rodriguez v. Union of
India. They argued that while Parliament can change the "basis" of a law,
it cannot directly overrule a judicial decision. The 2025 judgment was
founded on the fundamental right to "parity in promotional avenues" under
Article 14. By legislatively reinstating the "Glass Ceiling" for CAPF
officers, the State was committing a "Fraud on the Constitution." They
argued that the Bill was jurisdictionally provocative as it was
introduced while contempt proceedings against the MHA were pending.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued Parliamentary Supremacy. They contended that the
"Needs of the State" for IPS leadership in combat zones (like Bastar or
Siachen) were not adequately captured in the 2025 litigation. They argued
that Section 4 was a "Policy Choice" aimed at ensuring the "Uniformity of
National Internal Security Command." They maintained that Parliament
possesses the plenary power to regulate service conditions, and a
judicial decree cannot permanently "freeze" legislative competence.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (April 2026) issued a "Status Quo" order, observing
that a Bill cannot be used as a shield against contempt of a
constitutional court. A final hearing is set for May 2026.
cases.reasoning:
The Court's interim reasoning emphasized Constitutional Comity. The judge
noted that for a law to neutralize a judgment, it must remove the reason
for the judgment, not merely the result. The 2025 judgment was based on
the "Dignity and Career Expectations" of 10 lakh personnel. The 2026
Bill, by merely stating "IPS supremacy," failed to address the
constitutional inequality identified by the Court. The judge famously
remarked, "A legislative act that pronounces a court's judgment to be
wrong is an unconstitutional trespass into the judicial domain."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Non-Neutralization of Judicial
Mandates. It reinforces that Separation of Powers prevents the
Legislature from acting as an "Appellate Authority" over the Supreme
Court.

cases.title: State of Jharkhand v. Brajeshwar Singh, 2026
cases.facts:
Mr. Brajeshwar Singh, a retired government servant, was served an
administrative order in January 2026 deducting 15% of his pension for
five years. The order cited "unspecified irregularities" during his
tenure 15 years prior. No formal departmental inquiry was instituted; the
deduction was based on an executive "satisfaction" after a preliminary
audit. Singh challenged the order, arguing it violated the Jharkhand
Pension Rules and the Principles of Natural Justice.
cases.issues:
Can pension, recognized as "Property" under Article 300A, be deducted
through a summary executive order without a "Speaking Order"?

Does the lack of a "properly instituted departmental proceeding" render
the deduction void ab initio?

What is the limit of the State's power to punish a retiree for "stale"
allegations?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Singh)
The Petitioner argued that pension is not a "bounty" but a "deferred
wage." Relying on Deokinandan Prasad v. State of Bihar, he argued that
any deprivation of pension must follow strict Due Process. He contended
that Rule 43(b) of the Pension Rules requires a finding of "grave
misconduct" in a formal proceeding. A summary deduction based on
"allegations" 15 years old was characterized as Manifestly Arbitrary.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of Jharkhand)
The State argued "Sovereign Privilege." They contended that audits
discovered a massive financial leak during Singh's tenure, and the State
has an inherent right to recover public money. They argued that the 15%
deduction was a "lenient measure" compared to a full criminal
prosecution.
cases.judgment:
The High Court (March 2026) ruled in favor of Singh. The Court quashed
the deduction and ordered the State to refund the withheld amount with 9%
interest. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Administrative Transparency. The judge
ruled that "Reason is the heartbeat of a valid administrative act." A
one-line order citing "irregularities" fails the test of a Speaking
Order. The Court held that the State cannot bypass statutory rules (Rule
43b) by utilizing "preliminary audits" as a substitute for "departmental
inquiries." The judge reasoned that the "Right to Pension" is a
fundamental facet of the "Right to Life and Dignity" (Article 21), and
any clawback must be justified by proven, grave misconduct.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Speaking Order Requirement. It establishes that
administrative authorities must provide material evidence and specific
reasons when depriving a citizen of a vested financial right like a
pension.

cases.title: Laxmi Constructions v. Rent Authority, 2026
cases.facts:
The Supreme Court had issued a final eviction order against a tenant in a
prime commercial property. However, the tenant approached the local Rent
Authority (an administrative body), which passed a "Restoration Order"
effectively staying the Supreme Court's eviction decree, claiming the
property had a "title dispute." Laxmi Constructions, the landlord,
challenged this "stay" as an act of Administrative Usurpation.
cases.issues:
Can a subordinate administrative body "stay" or "overturn" a binding
judicial decree of a superior court?

What is the boundary between the "administrative finality" of a Rent
Authority and the "judicial supremacy" of the High Court/Supreme Court?

Does a Rent Authority have the jurisdiction to decide "Questions of
Title"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Landlord)
The Petitioner argued that the Rent Authority's action was a "contempt of
the hierarchy of law." They contended that under Article 141, the Supreme
Court's order is the law of the land. They argued that the Rent Authority
is a "creature of statute" with limited jurisdiction and cannot arrogate
to itself the power of a Civil Court to decide ownership.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Rent Authority)
The Authority argued that it was acting to prevent "Social Injustice."
They contended that new evidence regarding the landlord's title had
surfaced, and the Authority had an obligation to protect the tenant until
the "true owner" was identified.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (2026 INSC 475) ruled in favor of Laxmi Constructions.
The Court quashed the Rent Authority's order and imposed "Heavy Costs" on
the official who passed it. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a stern ruling on Institutional Discipline. The judge
ruled that the "Doctrine of Hierarchy" is essential for the Rule of Law.
If a subordinate body can stay a Supreme Court order, the entire judicial
system collapses into anarchy. The Court held that Rent Authorities are
limited to "Rent and Possession" issues; the moment a "Question of Title"
arises, the Authority is Coram Non Judice (not before a judge). The judge
famously noted, "Administrative zeal cannot be used as a cloak for
judicial insubordination."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Binding Precedent (Article 141). It
establishes that administrative and quasi-judicial bodies cannot exercise
powers that overreach into Civil Court jurisdictions or defy superior
judicial mandates.

cases.title: Frank Vitus v. NCB, 2024
cases.facts:
The Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) requested, and a trial court granted,
a bail condition requiring an accused (a foreign national) to share his
real-time location via a Google Maps "pin" 24/7 with the investigating
officer. The accused challenged this as an unconstitutional
administrative condition imposed under the guise of "procedural
safeguards."
cases.issues:
Can the State utilize "Digital Surveillance" as a mandatory condition for
bail under the CrPC?

Does a bail condition mandating continuous location sharing violate the
Right to Privacy under Article 21?

Does the Puttaswamy proportionality test apply to administrative/judicial
orders in criminal procedure?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Frank Vitus)
The Petitioner argued that "Liberty is not a trade-off for Privacy." He
contended that continuous tracking is a form of "Virtual Confinement" and
"Digital Shackling" that treats a non-convicted person as a laboratory
subject. Relying on Puttaswamy, he argued the measure was
disproportionate, as less intrusive means (like weekly reporting) were
available.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (NCB)
The NCB argued that foreign nationals are a "Flight Risk." They contended
that technology provides a "Humane Alternative" to prison. By
"consenting" to bail, the accused waived a portion of his privacy to
secure his liberty.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (July 2024) ruled in favor of Frank Vitus. The Court
struck down the "Google Maps" bail condition. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Digital Liberty. The judge ruled
that Bail is to ensure presence, not for constant surveillance. The Court
reasoned that "dropping a pin" creates a "Digital Panopticon" that fails
the proportionality test. The judge noted that the State cannot use
technology to execute "extra-statutory" monitoring that is not explicitly
authorized by law. The "Subjective Satisfaction" of the judge granting
bail must be governed by "Constitutional Morality," not "Technological
Convenience."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Proportionality Test for Bail Conditions. It
reinforces that Article 21 protects an individual from intrusive digital
monitoring by administrative or judicial authorities in the absence of a
specific law.

cases.title: Noble M. Paikada v. Union of India, 2024
cases.facts:
The Ministry of Environment (MoEFCC) issued a notification (Item 6)
granting a "Complete Exemption" from needing prior Environmental
Clearance (EC) for unearthing soil for "linear projects"
(roads/pipelines). This essentially allowed developers to bypass
ecological audits. A petitioner challenged this as a Mala Fide exercise
of power that violated the parent Environmental Protection Act (EPA).
cases.issues:
Can the Executive utilize "Delegated Power" to grant blanket exemptions
that defeat the very purpose of the parent Act?

Does an "unlimited exemption" constitute an Unconstitutional Delegation
of legislative power?

Is the "Subjective Satisfaction" of the Ministry regarding "National
Urgency" subject to the Wednesbury Principles?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Paikada)
The Petitioner argued that the parent EPA mandates the "Protection of the
Environment." By exempting soil excavation, the Ministry allowed the
destruction of fertile land without any oversight. They contended that an
exemption power cannot be used to "abrogate" the Act itself.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that road and pipeline projects are of "Extreme
National Importance." They contended that the "Administrative Speed"
required for these projects justified the exemption and that the Ministry
possessed the "Specialized Knowledge" to decide which activities were
"low impact."
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2024) ruled in favor of the Petitioner. The
Court struck down the exemption as "Vague, Arbitrary, and Illegal." The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Administrative Self-Restraint. The
judge ruled that "Exemption is the exception, not the rule." The Court
reasoned that the Ministry's notification was Ultra Vires because it did
not provide any "Intelligible Guidelines" on what kind of soil excavation
was safe. The judge held that the power of delegation must be exercised
to "Further the Object" of the Act, not to bypass it. Providing a blanket
exemption for "linear projects" without a "Rational Nexus" to
environmental safety was deemed Manifestly Arbitrary under Article 14.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Ultra Vires Doctrine. It establishes that
delegated legislation cannot be used to dismantle the core regulatory
framework of the parent Act, even in the interest of "Administrative
Efficiency."

cases.title: Md. Rahim Ali v. State of Assam, 2024
cases.facts:
The Border Police in Assam initiated proceedings against Mr. Ali,
doubting his nationality based on a "preliminary suspicion." A Foreigners
Tribunal passed an ex-parte order declaring him a foreigner because he
failed to produce documents from 1966. Ali challenged the "Subjective
Satisfaction" of the Tribunal, arguing that the proceedings were
initiated without any Prima Facie evidence of his foreign status.
cases.issues:
What is the "Standard of Material" required for an administrative body to
doubt a citizen's nationality?

Can an administrative tribunal rely on "Heads or Tails" logic (casting
the entire burden on the citizen) without the State first showing basic
grounds for doubt?

Does a "Reasonless Order" from a Tribunal violate Article 21?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Ali)
The Petitioner argued that nationality is a matter of "Life and Death."
He contended that the State must show "Relevant Material" before dragging
a person to a Tribunal. Relying on Sarbananda Sonowal, he argued that
"Burden of Proof" (Section 9 Foreigners Act) only shifts after the State
establishes a Prima Facie case.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of Assam)
The State argued that the Foreigners Act is a "Strict Liability" statute.
They contended that the "Subjective Satisfaction" of the Border Police is
enough to trigger an inquiry and that the Tribunal's decision is final on
facts.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (July 2024) ruled in favor of Ali. The Court quashed
the Tribunal order and quashed the initial doubt-proceedings. The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark judgment on Administrative Sanity. The
judge ruled that the "Power to Doubt" cannot be exercised "Capriciously."
The Court reasoned that the State had no material on record to doubt
Ali's citizenship other than his name and religion. The judge held that
"Subjective Satisfaction" must be based on Objective Evidence. Dragging a
person to a tribunal without any specific evidence is a violation of the
Principles of Natural Justice and Article 21. The Court warned against
Tribunals becoming "Instruments of Harassment."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Prima Facie Material Requirement for
citizenship inquiries. It reinforces that administrative discretion to
doubt status must be based on relevant material, protecting citizens from
arbitrary bureaucratic doubt.

cases.title: Kuldeep Kumar v. U.T. Chandigarh, 2024
cases.facts:
During the Chandigarh Mayoral elections, the Presiding Officer (an
administrative official) was caught on camera deliberately defacing eight
valid ballots cast for the AAP-Congress candidate, declaring them invalid
and announcing the BJP candidate as the winner. The "Presiding Officer's
Satisfaction" regarding the ballots was challenged in the Supreme Court.
cases.issues:
Is the "satisfaction" of an electoral presiding officer immune from
judicial review under the "Administrative Finality" of election law?

Can the Supreme Court utilize Article 142 to overturn an administrative
fraud and declare a winner directly?

What is the standard of "Accountability" for administrative officials
performing quasi-judicial electoral duties?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Kuldeep Kumar)
The Petitioner argued that the officer committed a "Murder of Democracy."
They contended that the "Administrative Record" was physically tampered
with by the official. Relying on the video evidence, they argued that the
Court must step in to "Set Right the Wrong" and maintain the public's
faith in the administration.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Official / State)
The official initially argued that the ballots were "dirty" or "marked."
The State argued that the correct remedy was an "Election Petition" in
the lower courts, not a direct writ to the Supreme Court, citing the
"Administrative Speed" of elections.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (February 2024) ruled in favor of Kuldeep Kumar. The
Court utilized Article 142, quashed the official result, and declared
Kuldeep Kumar as the duly elected Mayor. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a historic ruling on Electoral Accountability. The
judge ruled that "Administrative Finality" cannot be used as a "Cloak for
Fraud." The Court reasoned that when an official is caught "Red-Handed"
subverting the process, the High Court and Supreme Court have a Sovereign
Duty to intervene immediately. The judge held that the Presiding Officer
acted as an "Agent of a Political Party" rather than a "Neutral
Administrator," violating the Basic Structure of democracy.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Transparency Doctrine in Administration. It
reinforces that no administrative action, even in elections, is beyond
the "Long Arm of the Court" if it is proven to be fraudulent or mala
fide.

cases.title: Javed Ahmad Hajam v. State of Maharashtra, 2024
cases.facts:
Javed, a professor, posted a WhatsApp status criticizing the abrogation
of Article 370. The State Police initiated an FIR for "Promoting Enmity"
(Section 153A) and "Prejudicing Public Order." The Professor challenged
the FIR, arguing it was an Administrative Overreach designed to stifle
academic and personal critique.
cases.issues:
Can the State utilize "Criminal Machinery" to regulate "Private
Expression" on social media under the guise of "Administrative
Necessity"?

Does "Public Order" (Article 19(2)) allow the State to punish speech that
is merely "Critical" but not "Inciting"?

What is the threshold for the "Chilling Effect" in administrative law?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Hajam)
The Petitioner argued that "Dissent is the Safety Valve of Democracy." He
contended that his WhatsApp status was a "Subjective Opinion" shared with
his contacts. He argued that the State's administrative action (FIR) was
a "Misuse of Power" intended to create a "State of Fear" among
intellectuals.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of Maharashtra)
The State argued that in sensitive areas, even a "Status" can trigger a
"Chain Reaction" of violence. They contended that the police have the
"Subjective Satisfaction" to decide what constitutes a threat to "Public
Harmony."
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2024) ruled in favor of Hajam. The Court quashed
the criminal proceedings. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Constitutional Tolerance. The judge
ruled that "Every criticism is not an incitement." The Court reasoned
that the State cannot use the "Police Power" to enforce "Political
Uniformity." The judge held that "Public Order" must be interpreted
narrowly; unless there is a Proximity between the speech and violence,
administrative action is Ultra Vires Article 19(1)(a). The Court famously
remarked, "We must have a thick skin for dissent."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Narrow Interpretation of
Restrictions. It establishes that administrative authorities cannot
criminalize political critique by utilizing overbroad definitions of
"Public Order."

cases.title: DM, Gwalior v. National Insurance Co., 2026
cases.facts:
The District Election Officer (DM) "Requisitioned" a private bus for
election duty. While being driven by a government-appointed driver for
the administrative purpose of transporting voting machines, the bus met
with an accident. The Insurance Company refused to pay, arguing that once
the vehicle was "Requisitioned" by the State, the "Contract of Insurance"
was suspended, and the State assumed all risks.
cases.issues:
Upon "Administrative Requisition" (compulsory temporary seizure), does
the "Effective Control" of the asset shift entirely to the State?

Who is "Vicariously Liable" for accidents occurring during the discharge
of a public administrative duty?

Does the "Sovereign Function" defense protect the State from paying for
damages to requisitioned private property?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Insurance Co.)
The Petitioner argued that insurance is based on a "Private Risk
Profile." Requisitioning for election duty is an "Unforeseen Hazard"
imposed by the State. They contended that since the State had "Complete
Possession and Control," the State is the De Facto Owner for the duration
of the duty and must bear the liability.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (DM Gwalior)
The DM argued that the vehicle was still "Registered" in the private
owner's name. They contended that election duty is a "Sovereign Function"
and the State cannot be burdened with "Private Tortious Liability"
arising from routine traffic accidents.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (April 2026 INSC 455) ruled in favor of the Insurance
Company. The Court held the State Government absolutely liable for the
compensation. The Petitioner prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a definitive judgment on State Liability. The judge
ruled that "Control dictates Liability." The Court reasoned that when the
State forcibly takes possession of an asset for a "Public Purpose," the
State becomes the Temporary Owner. The judge held that the Sovereign
Immunity defense is obsolete in a welfare state. If the State breaks it
(or crashes it), the State pays for it. The Court held that the "Rule of
Law" requires the State to internalize the costs of its administrative
actions rather than shifting them to private citizens or insurers.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces State Tortious Liability. It establishes the legal
principle that upon administrative requisition, the State assumes
absolute liability for any harm or accidents involving the requisitioned
asset, reflecting the shift from "Sovereign Immunity" to "Administrative
Responsibility."

cases.title: In Re: Social Science Textbook (NCERT), 2026
cases.facts:
The NCERT (a statutory administrative body) published a revised Class 8
textbook which included a paragraph titled "The Slow Wheels of Justice,"
mentioning "Allegations of corruption in the higher judiciary" as a cause
for legal delays. The Supreme Court took Suo Moto cognizance, issued a
contempt notice to the administrative heads of NCERT, and ordered the
immediate ban of the textbook.
cases.issues:
Can the Judiciary review the "Academic Content" of textbooks developed by
an expert administrative body?

Does the "Freedom of Academic Expression" protect an administrative body
from Contempt of Court?

What is the standard for "Scandalising the Court" in the context of
institutional critique?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Supreme Court - Suo Moto)
The Court argued that the paragraph was "Calculated to Scrutinize and
Scandalise" the institution in the minds of children. They contended that
"Corruption" is a specific allegation that requires proof, and a blanket
mention in a textbook lowers the Dignity of the Court and the Rule of
Law.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (NCERT Officials)
The Officials argued that the textbook was written by an "Independent
Committee of Academics." They contended that "Academic Freedom" allows
for the discussion of institutional challenges. They argued there was no
Mala Fide intent to scandalize, but a goal to encourage critical thinking
about the justice system.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (February 2024) issued a "Contempt Notice" and ordered
a nationwide "Ban and Seizure" of the textbook. The Court prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Institutional Integrity. The judge
ruled that while "Critique" is allowed, "Vague and Scandalous
allegations" against the Judiciary in a state-sponsored textbook are
intolerable. The Court reasoned that the Dignity of the Judiciary is a
prerequisite for a functioning democracy. The judge held that the NCERT,
as an administrative arm of the State, has a "Duty of Care" to ensure
that it does not publish content that "Erodes Public Confidence" in the
third pillar of democracy.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Institutional Dignity Exception to Academic
Freedom. It reinforces the legal principle that administrative bodies
must adhere to strict standards of institutional respect when developing
national curricula, as "Scandalising the Court" remains a limit on
administrative expression.

cases.title: Union of India v. CyberAudit Collective
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Parliament passed the "National Cybersecurity Framework
Act." Section 89 of this Act empowered the Ministry of Electronics and
Information Technology (MeitY) to "frame rules to ensure the digital
sovereignty of India." Under this broad umbrella, MeitY notified the
"Critical Infrastructure Rules, 2026." Rule 4 of these new rules mandated
that all private cloud providers must grant the government "real-time,
mirrored access" to their servers without a judicial warrant, if the
Secretary deemed it a national emergency. The CyberAudit Collective, an
NGO, challenged Rule 4, arguing it was an instance of "Excessive
Delegation" where the Executive had usurped the "Essential Legislative
Function" of defining the scope of surveillance.
cases.issues:
Does Rule 4 constitute an unconstitutional abdication of "Essential
Legislative Functions" by the Parliament under the guise of delegation?

Can a delegated authority (the Ministry) create a rule that fundamentally
overrides existing statutory protections like the Right to Privacy?

What is the threshold for a "Policy Guideline" in a parent Act to prevent
a charge of excessive delegation?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (CyberAudit)
The Petitioners relied on the landmark judgment in In re Delhi Laws Act.
They argued that the Parliament cannot give the Executive a "blank
check." Section 89 provided no "intelligible guidelines" or "policy" on
how digital sovereignty should be protected. By creating a warrantless
surveillance regime, the Ministry was not just "filling in the details"
of the law; it was writing a new, draconian law. This constitutes a
violation of the Separation of Powers.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that in the hyper-fast realm of cybersecurity, the
Legislature lacks the technical expertise to define specific threats.
Relying on Avinder Singh v. State of Punjab, they argued for
"Administrative Pragmatism." They contended that "Digital Sovereignty"
was a sufficiently clear policy goal, and the Executive must have the
flexibility to create rules that respond to evolving cyber-warfare
tactics.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the CyberAudit Collective. Rule 4 was
struck down as ultra vires the parent Act and unconstitutional. The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a profound ruling on the Limits of Delegated
Legislation. The judge ruled that while "procedural" power can be
delegated, "policy" power cannot. Defining the conditions under which a
citizen's private data can be seized is an "Essential Legislative
Function." The judge reasoned that Section 89 of the Act was too vague to
act as a constitutional container. Since the parent Act did not
explicitly authorize warrantless mirrored access, the Executive could not
arrogate such power through the backdoor of rule-making.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Non-Abdication. It reinforces that
Essential Legislative Functions-those that affect fundamental rights or
the core policy of an Act-cannot be delegated to the Executive,
maintaining the primacy of the Legislature.

cases.title: Dr. Ananya v. National Medical Commission
cases.facts:
Dr. Ananya, a renowned neurosurgeon, had her license summarily cancelled
by the National Medical Commission (NMC) following a viral video alleging
she had accepted illegal kickbacks from a pharmaceutical firm. The NMC
invoked "Emergency Powers," cancelling the license without a show-cause
notice or an inquiry, citing "Public Morality." After the cancellation,
they offered her a "Review Hearing" thirty days later. Dr. Ananya
challenged this in the High Court, arguing that the failure to provide a
"Pre-Decisional Hearing" was a fatal blow to the Principles of Natural
Justice (Audi Alteram Partem).
cases.issues:
Can a "Post-Decisional Hearing" ever cure the lack of a "Pre-Decisional
Hearing" when a person's livelihood is at stake?

Does "Public Morality" or "Social Media Viralism" constitute a sufficient
"emergency" to bypass the Right to be Heard?

What is the scope of the "Doctrine of Civil Death" in administrative
suspensions?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Dr. Ananya)
The Petitioner argued that the cancellation of a professional license is
a "Civil Death." Relying on Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, she argued
that any procedure that deprives a person of their livelihood must be
"just, fair, and reasonable." A post-decisional hearing is a "meaningless
ritual" because the NMC has already formed a biased opinion. She
contended that a simple viral video does not create an "imminent threat
to life" that would justify dispensing with a 24-hour notice.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (NMC)
The NMC argued that the "integrity of the profession" was at stake. They
relied on Swadeshi Cotton Mills v. Union of India, asserting that in
cases of extreme public urgency, the requirements of natural justice can
be tailored or delayed. They argued that because a hearing was offered
eventually, the procedural defect was cured.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Dr. Ananya. The cancellation order was
quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a stern warning against "Administrative Impatience."
The judge ruled that the "right to be heard" is not a luxury that can be
discarded for the sake of public relations. The judge reasoned that a
post-decisional hearing can only be justified if the State can prove an
"immediate and irreparable harm." Acceptance of a bribe is a serious
allegation, but it does not prevent a surgeon from safely operating the
next morning. Therefore, there was no emergency. The Court held that the
NMC acted as a "moral vigilante" rather than a balanced administrative
body.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Requirement of a Pre-Decisional Hearing. It
establishes that the "Public Interest" exception to Natural Justice is
narrow and must be based on physical urgency, not reputational or moral
concerns.

cases.title: Apex Infra v. State of Karnataka
cases.facts:
The State Government issued a policy in 2024 promising a "10-year tax
holiday" to any company that built a waste-to-energy plant. Relying on
this, Apex Infra spent ₹500 Crores building a state-of-the-art facility.
In 2026, the government changed and issued a new notification withdrawing
the tax holiday for all existing plants, citing "fiscal deficit." Apex
Infra sued, claiming their "Legitimate Expectation" had been violated and
that the government was bound by "Equitable Estoppel."
cases.issues:
Can a "Policy Change" in the public interest override a specific
"Promise" made to an individual investor?

What is the distinction between a "Procedural" and a "Substantive"
Legitimate Expectation?

Under what circumstances can the State renege on a financial incentive
used to induce private investment?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Apex Infra)
The Petitioner relied on Food Corporation of India v. Kamdhenu Cattle
Feed Industries. They argued that "Legitimate Expectation" is a facet of
Article 14 (Anti-Arbitrariness). Once a citizen alters their position to
their detriment based on a State promise, the State cannot act like a
"deceptive private trader." They argued that a "Fiscal Deficit" is a
foreseeable administrative reality and not a "supervening public
interest" sufficient to break a solemn promise.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State)
The State argued that no government can "freeze" the sovereign power of
taxation or policy-making for the future. They relied on Kasinka Trading
v. Union of India, arguing that policy is dynamic. They contended that
"Legitimate Expectation" is not a vested right and must yield to the
larger public good of managing the state exchequer.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Apex Infra. The Court ordered the
State to honor the tax holiday for the duration promised. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on State Accountability. The judge
ruled that the State is not immune from the requirement of "Fairness."
The judge reasoned that while the State can change policy, it must
provide a "Transition Period" or honor existing commitments that induced
specific investments. To withdraw the benefit midway through a 10-year
period is "Manifestly Arbitrary" and violates the citizen's trust in the
law. The judge held that the "Public Interest" in state revenue is
balanced by the "Public Interest" in the sanctity of the State's word.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case solidifies the Substantive Doctrine of Legitimate Expectation.
It establishes that the State is bound by its promises if a citizen has
acted upon them, and a mere "change of government" or "fiscal need" is
not a valid excuse to break that trust.

cases.title: The Citizen v. The Lokpal
cases.facts:
A citizen filed a corruption complaint against a Union Minister. The
Lokpal, after a preliminary inquiry, closed the case, stating in a one-
line order: "We are satisfied that there are no grounds to proceed." No
reasons were provided. The citizen filed a writ of Certiorari, arguing
that the "Subjective Satisfaction" of the Lokpal must be based on
objective material and that the failure to provide reasons (a "Speaking
Order") made the decision unchallengeable and thus arbitrary.
cases.issues:
Is the "Subjective Satisfaction" of a high-level ombudsman immune from
judicial review?

Does the "Right to Reason" (Speaking Orders) form a part of the
Principles of Natural Justice in quasi-judicial proceedings?

Can the Court compel an administrative body to disclose the "material"
upon which its satisfaction was based?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Citizen)
The Petitioner relied on S.N. Mukherjee v. Union of India. He argued that
"Reason is the heartbeat of a decision." Without reasons, a decision is a
"blanket of silence" that hides potential bias or political pressure. He
contended that the Lokpal, as a public watchdog, has an even higher duty
of transparency than a regular court.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Lokpal)
The Lokpal argued that the statute gave them "unfettered discretion" to
decide whether a prima facie case exists. They contended that in
sensitive corruption cases involving high-ranking officials, providing
detailed reasons could "prejudice the investigation" or "tip off the
accused" if the case were reopened later.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Citizen. The one-line order was
quashed, and the Lokpal was directed to pass a "Speaking Order." The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a definitive judgment on Administrative Transparency.
The judge ruled that the days of "Inscrutable Satisfaction" are over. In
a democracy, every exercise of power must be "Accountable." The judge
reasoned that reasons are the "link between the mind of the decision-
maker and the actual controversy." Without reasons, the High Court cannot
perform its constitutional duty of judicial review. The judge held that
"Confidentiality" can be maintained through "Redacted Orders," but "Total
Silence" is the hallmark of an arbitrary power, which the Constitution
does not recognize.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Mandatory Requirement of Speaking Orders. It
establishes that all quasi-judicial bodies must provide a "Reasoned
Decision" to ensure they have applied their minds to the material on
record and to allow for effective judicial oversight.

cases.title: Metro-Link v. The Land Acquisition Authority
cases.facts:
The Land Acquisition Authority issued an order to seize a historic
library to build an entry point for a new Metro station. The Metro-Link
company provided an alternative design that used a vacant government
parking lot 50 meters away, which would save the library but cost ₹10
Crores more. The Authority rejected the alternative, stating that the law
gives them "absolute discretion" to choose the cheapest site. The Library
Trust challenged this under the "Doctrine of Proportionality."
cases.issues:
Is the "Wednesbury Test" (only intervening if the decision is "so absurd
that no reasonable person could make it") still the only standard for
reviewing administrative discretion in India?

Can the Court substitute its own "Reasoning" for that of the Executive
when a fundamental interest (culture/heritage) is at stake?

Does the Proportionality Test allow the Court to look at the "merits" of
an administrative choice?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Library Trust)
The Petitioners relied on Om Kumar v. Union of India. They argued that
the Court must move from "Secondary Review" (Wednesbury) to "Primary
Review" (Proportionality). They contended that the "End" (Metro access)
did not justify the "Means" (destruction of a library) when a less-
restrictive alternative existed. Saving ₹10 Crores is not a sufficient
"State Interest" to destroy a unique public asset.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Authority)
The Authority argued that they are the "sole judges" of public utility
and budget. They contended that "Proportionality" would allow judges to
become "Super-Administrators" and "Super-Engineers," which violates the
separation of powers. They argued the decision met the "Wednesbury Test"
because it was a "rational choice" based on fiscal prudence.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Library Trust. The acquisition was
quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark judgment on Substantive Review. The judge
ruled that for decisions involving "Significant Interests" (like heritage
or environment), the Proportionality Test is the correct standard. The
judge reasoned that the State must show that (1) the aim was legitimate,
(2) the measure was suitable, and (3) it was Necessary (the least
restrictive means). Since the parking lot alternative was viable and only
marginally more expensive, the State's choice to destroy the library was
"Disproportionate."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Primacy of Proportionality over Wednesbury
Unreasonableness in matters affecting public assets. It establishes the
legal principle that administrative discretion must choose the "Least
Harmful Path" when exercising power.

cases.title: State of Bihar v. The Judicial Reform Union
cases.facts:
The State Government of Bihar established a "Judicial Infrastructure
Committee" to oversee the construction of new courtrooms. The Committee
was chaired by the State Law Secretary (an executive officer) but was
given the power to decide "Contempt of Committee" and punish individuals
for "interfering with its administrative work." A lawyer was fined for
critiquing the committee's budget allocation. He challenged the fine,
alleging "Institutional Bias"-arguing that the Committee was acting as
the prosecutor, the complainant, and the judge in its own cause.
cases.issues:
Can an administrative committee possess the power to punish for its own
contempt?

Does the combination of "investigative" and "adjudicative" functions in a
single executive body violate the Rule against Bias?

What is the threshold for "Actual Bias" vs. a "Real Likelihood of Bias"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Lawyer)
The Petitioner relied on A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India. He argued that
"Justice must not only be done, but must be seen to be done." The Law
Secretary had a "personal stake" in defending the budget he drafted. By
acting as the judge of the person critiquing him, he violated the most
sacred rule of Administrative Law: Nemo judex in causa sua.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State)
The State argued that the Committee was not a "Court" and therefore not
bound by the strict separation of functions. They contended that
"Administrative Speed" required the Committee to have disciplinary powers
to prevent obstructionists from stalling court construction. They argued
that "Actual Bias" was not proven.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Lawyer. The fine was quashed, and
the "Contempt" power of the committee was struck down. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a rigorous ruling on Administrative Fairness. The
judge ruled that the rule against bias applies to every body performing a
quasi-judicial function. The judge reasoned that the "Real Likelihood of
Bias" is the test. A reasonable person would believe that a Law Secretary
cannot be impartial when judging a critic of his own work. The Court held
that "Efficiency" is no excuse for "Injustice." The judge famously
remarked, "The Executive cannot be allowed to carve out its own tiny
kingdoms of judicial power where it is both the master and the judge."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Rule against Bias (Nemo judex in causa sua). It
establishes the legal principle that investigative and adjudicative
powers cannot be housed in the same administrative officer, and that even
a "likelihood" of bias is sufficient to invalidate a decision.

cases.title: Tech-Giant v. The Competition Authority
cases.facts:
The "Digital Markets Act, 2026" contained a "Finality Clause" (Section
112) which stated: "Every order of the Competition Authority regarding
market fines shall be final and shall not be called into question in any
court of law by way of appeal or otherwise." The Authority imposed a
₹1,000 Crore fine on a Tech-Giant. The company filed a writ of
Certiorari, alleging an "Error of Law apparent on the face of the
record." The Authority argued that the High Court's jurisdiction was
"Ousted" by Section 112.
cases.issues:
Can an "Ouster Clause" (Finality Clause) in a statute strip the High
Courts of their power of Judicial Review under Article 226?

Does the Basic Structure Doctrine prevent the Parliament from making an
administrative order "Un-challengeable"?

What is the difference between a "Statutory Right of Appeal" and
"Constitutional Judicial Review"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Tech-Giant)
The Petitioner relied on L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India. They argued
that Judicial Review is an un-amendable feature of the Basic Structure. A
statute can take away a "right to appeal" to a higher tribunal, but it
can never take away the High Court's constitutional power to issue writs.
If the Authority commits a "Jurisdictional Error," the Court must
intervene to maintain the Rule of Law.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Authority)
The Authority argued for "Legislative Supremacy." They contended that the
"New Economy" requires speed and finality. If every fine is tied up in
the High Courts for decades, the Act becomes a "Dead Letter." They argued
that Parliament had the right to choose "Expert Finality" over "Judicial
Procrastination."
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Tech-Giant. The Court held that
Section 112 could not block a Writ Petition. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a firm ruling on Constitutional Supremacy. The judge
ruled that the Parliament is a "creature of the Constitution" and cannot
destroy the "Check and Balance" system. The judge reasoned that an Ouster
Clause is like a "No Entry" sign for a side-road (appeal), but the High
Court possesses a "Constitutional Master-Key" (writs). The judge held
that even if a statute says an order is "Final," the Court can always
review it on three grounds: (1) Lack of Jurisdiction, (2) Violation of
Natural Justice, and (3) Error of Law. To allow an authority to be
"Final" in the sense of being "Above the Law" would be to invite
administrative tyranny.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Inalienability of Judicial Review. It
establishes the legal principle that no Act of Parliament can oust the
Writ Jurisdiction of the High Courts, ensuring that every administrative
authority remains "Under the Law."

cases.title: Union of India v. The Refugee Rights Union
cases.facts:
In 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued an administrative circular
mandating the "Deportation of all unregistered foreign nationals in
District X within 48 hours." The circular gave the local police the
"Subjective Satisfaction" to decide who was unregistered without a
documentation check. The Refugee Rights Union challenged this, arguing
the circular was "Manifestly Arbitrary" under Article 14 and lacked a
"Proximity of Reason" to the stated goal of national security.
cases.issues:
Can an administrative order dispense with a "Standard of Proof" under the
guise of national security?

Does "Manifest Arbitrariness" serve as a ground for striking down
executive action even if no specific statutory rule is violated?

What is the threshold for the "Reasonable Basis" of executive
satisfaction?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Union)
The Petitioner relied on E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu and Shayara
Bano v. Union of India. They argued that "Equality" and "Arbitrariness"
are sworn enemies. Giving the police the power to deport based on "visual
suspicion" rather than a "documentary audit" is the height of
arbitrariness. There is no rational nexus between the "Means" (random
deportation) and the "End" (security).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (MHA)
The Government argued "Sovereign Privilege." They contended that
"District X" was a high-risk zone and that the "Subjective Satisfaction"
of the local police-who know the terrain-is more valuable than a slow,
legalistic audit. They argued the Court should not interfere in matters
of "External Security."
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Refugee Rights Union. The circular
was struck down as unconstitutional. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Procedural Sanity. The judge ruled that
