"Satisfaction" cannot be a "Whim." The judge reasoned that for an
administrative act to be valid, there must be a "Proximity of Evidence."
To deport a person, the State must have at least some objective material
(like an expired visa). The judge held that the circular was "Manifestly
Arbitrary" because it lacked a "Determining Principle"-it essentially
authorized the police to act on prejudice. The judge famously remarked,
"National Security is a shield, not a mask for administrative
lawlessness."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Manifest Arbitrariness. It
establishes the legal principle that every executive order must have an
"Objective Basis," and that "National Security" does not grant the State
the power to act without a rational and evidentiary foundation.

cases.title: DM, Varanasi v. The Street Vendors Collective
cases.facts:
The Parliament passed the "Town Planning Act," which empowered the "State
Urban Authority" to issue vending licenses. The State Urban Authority,
being overwhelmed, issued a sub-notification delegating its license-
issuing power to the "Local District Magistrate" (DM). The DM, in turn,
delegated this power to a "Private Security Agency" to manage the street
vendors. The Vendors challenged this, invoking the maxim "Delegatus non
potest delegare" (A delegate cannot further delegate).
cases.issues:
Does the principle of "Sub-Delegation" require express authorization in
the parent Act?

Can a "Public Function" (licensing) be delegated to a "Private Entity"?

Is a sub-delegation void if it bypasses the "Expertise" required by the
parent Act?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Vendors)
The Petitioner argued that the Parliament trusted the "Urban Authority"
because of its expertise. The Authority could not "abdicate" its duty to
a DM, and the DM certainly could not hand it over to a private company.
They argued the maxim Delegatus non potest delegare is absolute unless
the statute says "The Authority or its nominee."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (DM)
The DM argued "Administrative Necessity." He contended that with 50,000
vendors, the DM's office lacked the manpower and therefore "hired" the
private agency as a "technical facilitator." He argued this was not a
"delegation of power" but a "hiring of service."
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Street Vendors. The sub-delegation
to the private agency was quashed as illegal. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fundamental lesson on Administrative
Accountability. The judge ruled that Public Power is a Trust. The judge
reasoned that unless the parent Act explicitly allows sub-delegation, it
is strictly prohibited. The reasoning was that the "Mind" of the delegate
is what the law requires; the DM cannot replace the "Expert Mind" of the
Urban Authority with the "Profit-seeking Mind" of a private security
firm. The judge held that a private agency has no constitutional
accountability, and delegating the power to grant or deny a "Right to
Livelihood" to them is an unconstitutional surrender of state duty.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Rule against Sub-Delegation (Delegatus non
potest delegare). It establishes that administrative power must be
exercised by the body specified in the law, and any further delegation is
void ab initio without explicit statutory permission.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Heritage Restoration Society
cases.facts:
The Ministry of Railways appointed a "Technical Expert Committee" to
decide if an 18th-century heritage bridge should be demolished for a
high-speed rail line. The Committee comprised four structural engineers
but no historians or conservationists. The Committee recommended
demolition. The Heritage Society challenged the "Composition" of the
Committee, arguing that an "Administrative Expert Body" must reflect the
"Inter-disciplinary nature" of the task.
cases.issues:
Does the Court have the power to review the "Composition" of an
administrative expert committee?

What constitutes a "Relevant Consideration" that an administrative body
must take into account?

Can an administrative decision be quashed if it is "Expertly One-sided"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Society)
The Petitioner argued that a bridge is not just a "structure" but a
"monument." By excluding conservationists, the Ministry ensured a biased
"Engineering-only" outcome. They argued that the Ministry failed to take
into account a "Relevant Consideration" (Cultural Heritage), making the
decision "legally perverse."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union)
The Government argued that they had "Absolute Discretion" to choose their
experts. They contended that "Engineering Safety" was the primary concern
and that the Court should not interfere in the technical choice of
personnel. They argued the decision was a "Policy Decision" beyond
judicial reach.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Heritage Restoration Society. The
demolition was stayed, and the Ministry was ordered to reconstitute the
committee. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a sophisticated judgment on "The Quality of Decision-
making." The judge ruled that while the Court won't substitute its
opinion for an expert's, it will ensure the "Decision-making Process" was
comprehensive. The judge reasoned that a bridge of 300 years possesses
multiple "Constitutional Identities"-it is property, it is
infrastructure, and it is "Heritage" (Article 49). To exclude the
"Heritage" aspect by excluding historians is to commit an "Exclusion of
Relevant Material." The judge held that an "Expert Committee" must be
"Fit for the Purpose," and a one-sided committee leads to an arbitrary
result.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case expands the Judicial Review of the Decision-making Process. It
establishes the legal principle that administrative bodies must include
"Inter-disciplinary Experts" for complex tasks, and the failure to
consider all relevant facets of a problem (e.g., historical vs.
engineering) renders a decision "Unreasonable" and "Void."

cases.title: Union of India v. The Algorithmic Justice Project
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Ministry of Finance implemented "Tax-Sentinel," an AI system
designed to automatically freeze bank accounts of individuals flagged for
"high-probability tax evasion." The system analyzed petabytes of
transaction data, social media activity, and travel history. Mr. Gupta's
accounts were frozen without notice. When he inquired, the Department
stated they could not provide the specific reasons because the AI's "Deep
Learning" logic was proprietary and "unexplainable" even to the
developers. The Algorithmic Justice Project filed a writ, arguing that
"unexplainable" administrative action is the antithesis of the Rule of
Law.
cases.issues:
Can the State rely on "Black-Box" algorithms to take adverse actions
against citizens if the logic cannot be explained in human-readable form?

Does the requirement of a "Speaking Order" apply to decisions generated
by an AI?

Does "Proprietary Trade Secret" privilege of a private developer override
the citizen's right to know the grounds of an administrative decision?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Justice Project)
The Petitioners relied on the Third Principle of Natural Justice: the
duty to give reasons. They argued that "Reason is the soul of the law."
If a machine cannot explain why it took a person's property, the decision
is Manifestly Arbitrary under Article 14. They contended that the State
cannot delegate sovereign coercive power to a non-transparent private
algorithm.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that Tax-Sentinel was 99% accurate and essential to
combat sophisticated financial crimes. They argued that requiring
"explainability" would force the government to use inferior, simpler
technology, aiding tax evaders. They asserted that the "Subjective
Satisfaction" of the AI was based on objective data patterns that no
human could process.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Justice Project. The Court held
that every AI-generated administrative order must be accompanied by a
human-intelligible "Impact Statement" explaining the key factors behind
the decision. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Digital Natural Justice. The
judge ruled that "Algorithm is not a sovereign." If the State adopts an
automated system, the State assumes the burden of making that system's
logic transparent. A "Speaking Order" is a constitutional requirement
under Article 14 and 21; "I don't know, the AI decided it" is not a legal
reason. The Court held that any administrative system that is
"unexplainable" is ipso facto arbitrary.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Algorithmic Transparency. It
reinforces that quasi-judicial and adverse administrative actions must
have a "Reasonable Basis" that is communicable to the affected party,
regardless of the technology used.

cases.title: State of Maharashtra v. The Tech-Unions
cases.facts:
The State Government issued "The Gig-Worker Welfare Rules" in January
2026. However, Clause 1(b) of the rules stated that the mandatory
insurance premiums for the last three years (2023-2025) must be paid by
platforms by March 2026. The Tech-Unions challenged this, arguing that
Subordinate Legislation cannot impose liabilities retrospectively unless
the Parent Act specifically grants the power to do so.
cases.issues:
Can an executive rule-making body exercise retrospective power in the
absence of an express provision in the parent statute?

What is the difference between a "Retrospective Law" (passed by
Parliament) and a "Retrospective Rule" (passed by the Executive)?

Does imposing past financial liabilities violate the Doctrine of Vested
Rights?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Tech-Unions)
The Petitioners relied on Hukam Chand v. Union of India. They argued that
the power to legislate retrospectively is a "Sovereign Power" that
belongs only to the Parliament/Legislature. Subordinate authorities are
"creatures of the Act" and cannot go beyond the powers delegated to them.
Since the parent Act was silent on retrospectivity, the rule was Ultra
Vires.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State)
The State argued that the rules were "Remedial" in nature, designed to
correct the historical exploitation of workers. They contended that the
"Public Interest" in social security for the poor overrides the
commercial "Vested Rights" of multi-billion dollar platforms.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Tech-Unions. Clause 1(b) was struck
down to the extent of its retrospectivity. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a classic ruling on Delegated Legislation. The judge
ruled that the Executive has no "inherent" power to make retrospective
rules. Retrospectivity is an extreme power that must be "Expressly
Delegated" by the Legislature. The judge reasoned that businesses plan
their finances based on existing laws; allowing the Executive to reach
back into the past and create new liabilities would destroy "Commercial
Certainty" and violate the Rule of Law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Rule against Retrospectivity in Delegated
Legislation. It establishes that rules and regulations are always
prospective unless the parent statute explicitly authorizes retrospective
application.

cases.title: Mehta v. The Civil Aviation Authority
cases.facts:
Mr. Mehta, a pilot, had his license suspended by the Civil Aviation
Authority (CAA) after a minor runway incursion. The inquiry committee
that suspended him was chaired by the very same official who had designed
the runway markings that Mehta claimed were confusing and led to the
accident. Mehta alleged "Subjective Bias" and "Conflict of Interest." The
CAA argued that as a technical body, only their internal experts could
judge flight safety.
cases.issues:
Does "Departmental Expertise" override the rule against Institutional
Bias?

What constitutes a "Real Likelihood of Bias" in an administrative
inquiry?

Can a person act as a judge in a dispute where their own professional
work is being questioned?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mehta)
The Petitioner relied on A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India. He argued that
"Justice must not only be done but seen to be done." If the judge has a
stake in proving the runway was perfectly designed, he cannot be
impartial in judging the pilot who blames the design. This was a textbook
case of Official Bias.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (CAA)
The CAA argued the Doctrine of Necessity. They contended that all senior
officials in the CAA are involved in design and regulation, and bringing
in an outside judge would compromise the "Technical Integrity" of the
safety audit.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Mr. Mehta. The inquiry was quashed, and
a fresh committee with independent experts was ordered. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a rigorous ruling on Administrative Fairness. The
judge ruled that the Rule against Bias is a "Universal Human Right." The
judge reasoned that the Chairman had a "psychological and professional
interest" in exonerating his own design. While "Necessity" is a defense,
it did not apply here because independent pilots or retired judges could
have been co-opted. The judge famously remarked, "A judge cannot be a
witness to his own perfection."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Bias (Nemo judex in causa sua). It
establishes that the slightest suspicion of a personal or professional
stake in the outcome disqualifies an administrative officer from
adjudicating, ensuring the "Cold Neutrality" of the law.

cases.title: Green-Build v. The Environmental Tribunal
cases.facts:
The Environmental Tribunal (NGT) issued a "Standard Operating Procedure"
(SOP) mandating that all construction within 500 meters of a lake must
use "Carbon-Negative Cement." Green-Build challenged this, providing
scientific evidence that such cement was not yet structurally viable for
high-rises. The Tribunal argued it possessed "Expert Discretion" to set
environmental standards to protect the Right to a Clean Environment
(Article 21).
cases.issues:
Can a quasi-judicial Tribunal issue broad "policy-like" SOPs that affect
a whole industry?

What is the scope of Judicial Review over the technical decisions of an
"Expert Body"?

Does the Precautionary Principle allow an authority to mandate unproven
technology?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Green-Build)
The Petitioners argued that the Tribunal was "Judicially Legislating."
They contended that while the NGT is an expert body, its orders must be
"Reasonable" and "Implementable." Mandating an experimental material was
Manifestly Unreasonable and a violation of the Freedom of Trade (Article
19(1)(g)).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Tribunal)
The Tribunal argued that "Environment is the Supreme Interest." Relying
on the Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum case, they argued that the
Precautionary Principle mandates acting even in the absence of scientific
certainty to prevent ecological collapse.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Green-Build. The SOP was "read down"
to be a recommendation rather than a mandatory rule. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Administrative Balance. The judge ruled
that "Expertise is not a license for irrationality." The judge reasoned
that while Tribunals have broad powers, they cannot ignore "Physical and
Economic Impossibility." Forcing an industry to use dangerous or non-
existent material fails the Wednesbury Test of Reasonableness. The Court
held that "Sustainable Development" requires a balance between ecology
and structural safety.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Limits of Expert Discretion. It reinforces that
quasi-judicial orders must be "Proportional" and "Reasonable," and that
technical bodies are not exempt from the standard of feasibility in
administrative law.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Whistleblower
cases.facts:
An anonymous whistleblower leaked a "Confidential Audit Report" showing
massive corruption in a defense deal. The State moved to suppress the
report in court, invoking Section 123 of the Evidence Act (State
Privilege) and the "National Security" exception in Administrative Law.
The whistleblower filed an application for the "Production of Documents,"
arguing the report proved a fraud on the exchequer.
cases.issues:
Is the "Subjective Satisfaction" of a Minister regarding "State
Privilege" final and non-justiciable?

Can the Court perform an "In-Camera" inspection of documents the State
claims are "Secret"?

Does the "Public Interest in Justice" outweigh the "Public Interest in
Secrecy" when corruption is alleged?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Union of India)
The Government argued that defense audits are "Classified" and their
disclosure would aid enemy nations. They relied on the "Crown Privilege"
doctrine, asserting that the Executive is the sole judge of what
constitutes a "State Secret."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Whistleblower)
The Respondent relied on S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges
Case). They argued that "Transparency is the rule, Secrecy the
exception." They contended that "National Security" cannot be used as a
"Burial Ground" for evidence of corruption.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Whistleblower. The Court ordered
an In-Camera inspection and subsequently allowed the document into
evidence. The Respondent prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a definitive ruling on Executive Transparency. The
judge ruled that the Court-not the Executive-is the final arbiter of
"Privilege." [Image showing the concept of Checks and Balances in
government] The judge reasoned that the State has no privilege to hide
"Illegality." If a document shows a "Prima Facie Case of Fraud," the
interest of the public in a clean administration is superior to
administrative confidentiality. The judge famously noted, "Sunlight is
the best disinfectant."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Judicial Oversight of State
Privilege. It establishes that no administrative document is immune from
the Court's gaze if justice requires its production, limiting the
"National Security" defense in corruption cases.

cases.title: The Media Collective v. The IT Registrar
cases.facts:
The IT Registrar, an administrative official, issued an order permanently
banning an independent news portal "IndiNews" for "publishing content
that could potentially cause communal disharmony." The Registrar relied
on a single controversial article. IndiNews challenged the ban as
"Disproportionate," arguing that the State should have ordered the
removal of the article rather than the destruction of the entire portal.
cases.issues:
Is the "Doctrine of Proportionality" applicable to administrative orders
restricting Freedom of Expression?

Can the State use "Sovereign Discretion" to choose the most "drastic
measure" if a "softer measure" is available?

What is the standard for judicial review of "Preventive Administrative
Actions"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Media)
The Petitioners relied on Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India. They argued
that a "Permanent Ban" is a "Digital Capital Punishment." They contended
that the State must follow the "Least Restrictive Measure" test. Banning
a whole website for one article is like "burning the house to roast a
pig."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Registrar)
The State argued that in the "Viral Era," a single article can trigger a
riot in minutes. They contended that "Public Order" (Article 19(2))
grants the Executive the power to take "Decisive and Final Action" to
maintain peace.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Media Collective. The permanent
ban was quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Administrative Proportionality.
The judge ruled that the State must pass the Four-Fold Test of
Proportionality: (1) Legitimate Goal, (2) Suitability, (3) Necessity
(Least Restrictive), and (4) Balancing. The judge reasoned that while the
goal of communal peace was legitimate, the "Necessity" prong failed. The
State could have blocked the specific URL. A "Total Ban" was an
"Executive Overreach" that killed a legitimate trade ( journalism) to
solve a localized problem.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Primordial Status of Proportionality in
Administrative Law. It confirms that State actions affecting fundamental
rights must be "Narrowly Tailored," and the judiciary will strike down
any "Sledgehammer" approach to governance.

cases.title: State of Bihar v. The Contractual Teachers
cases.facts:
The State Government hired 50,000 "Contractual Teachers" to work in the
same schools as "Regular Teachers." The contractual teachers performed
the same duties, taught the same hours, and had the same qualifications,
but were paid 40% less. The State argued this was a "Policy Choice" based
on their "Budgetary Constraints" and that the teachers had "consented" to
the lower pay by signing the contract.
cases.issues:
Can the State use "Budgetary Constraints" as a valid defense for
discriminatory pay scales?

Does "Equal Pay for Equal Work" form a part of the Rule of Law and Non-
Arbitrariness under Article 14?

Can a citizen "waive" their right to equal treatment by signing a
contract of employment?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Teachers)
The Petitioners relied on State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh. They argued
that "Equal Pay for Equal Work" is an "Inherent Facet of Human Dignity."
They contended that the State, as a "Model Employer," cannot practice
"Economic Exploitation" under the guise of "Contractual Freedom."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State)
The State argued that regular teachers were part of a "Cadre" with
different recruitment processes. They contended that "Pay-Parity" would
result in an additional ₹10,000 Crore burden on the exchequer, siphoning
money from schools and mid-day meals.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Teachers. The Court ordered the
State to implement pay parity within one year. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a defining ruling on Administrative Equality. The
judge ruled that Article 14 is a "Dynamic Equality." If the "Duties and
Responsibilities" are identical, a difference in "Recruitment Label" is a
"Fake Classification" that has no "Rational Nexus" to the work. The judge
reasoned that the State cannot use its "Dominant Position" to force
citizens into unconscionable contracts. The judge famously stated,
"Budgetary constraints cannot be a license for unconstitutional
discrimination."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case enshrines the Doctrine of the State as a Model Employer. It
establishes that Equal Pay for Equal Work is a binding Administrative
mandate, and that fiscal convenience is not a ground to violate the
guarantee of Equality.

cases.title: The Citizen v. The Ministry of Railways
cases.facts:
The Ministry of Railways issued a "Technical Policy" stating that all
manual railway crossings would be replaced by "Remote-AI Signal Boxes." A
local village association challenged the policy, showing data that in
their foggy region, AI sensors frequently failed, leading to accidents.
They demanded a human guard. The Ministry argued the Court has zero power
to review "Technical Engineering Policies."
cases.issues:
What is the limit of Judicial Review over "Technical and Scientific
Policy" of the State?

Can the Court intervene if a "Scientific Choice" results in a direct
threat to the Right to Life (Article 21)?

Does the Doctrine of Deference require the Court to always believe the
"State Expert"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Village)
The Petitioners argued that Article 21 is a "High-Priority Right." They
contended that "Science" is not "Infallible." By ignoring localized
weather data, the Ministry's policy was "Manifestly Irrational" and
endangered human lives.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Ministry)
The Government argued the "Doctrine of Separation of Powers." They
contended that judges are "Legal Experts," not "Signal Engineers." If the
Court starts reviewing sensor technology, it will paralyze national
infrastructure modernization.
cases.judgment:
The High Court issued a "Mandatory Direction." It upheld the policy
generally but ordered "Human Redundancy" in high-fog zones. The Plaintiff
partially prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a balanced judgment on Expert Accountability. The
judge ruled that while the Court will generally show "Deference" to
experts, it will not show "Blind Faith." The judge reasoned that "Policy"
must be "Evidence-Based." Since the Village proved that the AI failed in
specific conditions, the Ministry's "One-size-fits-all" approach was
"Arbitrary." The Court held that the Right to Life (Article 21) is the
"Metric of All Policy." Any technological leap that ignores "Foreseeable
Risks to Life" is subject to judicial correction.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the "Hard Look" Doctrine in Judicial Review. It
reinforces that technical policies are subject to review if they are
irrational or endanger fundamental rights, ending the era of absolute
technical immunity for the Executive.

cases.title: Apex Pharma v. The Drug Controller
cases.facts:
The Drug Controller cancelled the 20-year manufacturing license of Apex
Pharma because they found a labeling error on one batch of vitamin
tablets (the font size was 1mm smaller than required). Apex Pharma argued
this was a "Minor Technical Infringement." The Controller argued they had
"Absolute Discretion" to cancel licenses for any violation of the Drugs
and Cosmetics Act.
cases.issues:
Is the "Cancellation of License" a Proportional Punishment for a minor
labeling error?

Does the "Right to Trade" (Article 19(1)(g)) protect a business from
"Administrative Over-Kill"?

What is the threshold for "Abuse of Discretion" in penalizing
administrative infractions?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Apex Pharma)
The Petitioners argued the "Sledgehammer Doctrine." They contended that a
"Fine" would have been sufficient. By killing the entire business for a
"Printer's Error," the State acted with "Wednesbury Irrationality" and
destroyed the livelihood of 500 employees.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Controller)
The State argued "Zero Tolerance for Drugs." They contended that
"Labeling" is a critical safety requirement and that allowing "small
errors" would lead to a "Slippery Slope" where companies ignore all
safety standards.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Apex Pharma. The cancellation was
replaced by a "Nominal Fine." The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a definitive judgment on Substantive Fairness. The
judge ruled that "The punishment must fit the crime." The judge reasoned
that "Absolute Discretion" does not mean "Capricious Power." Under the
Doctrine of Proportionality, the State must choose the "Least Restrictive
Punishment" that achieves the goal of compliance. Since the tablets
themselves were safe, a total ban was "Shocking to the Conscience of the
Court."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Proportionality in Administrative
Penalties. It establishes that the State cannot impose "Existential
Penalties" for "Minor Infractions," protecting the economic rights of
citizens from administrative excessive zeal.

cases.title: The Students Union v. The University Registrar
cases.facts:
The University Registrar rusticated five students for "Anti-University
Activities" after they organized a protest against a 200% fee hike. The
students were not given a chance to see the "Security Report" that
allegedly proved they incited violence. The Registrar argued that
"University Discipline" is an internal administrative matter based on his
"Subjective Satisfaction" and is beyond the reach of civil courts.
cases.issues:
Is the "Internal Discipline" of a State-funded University subject to
Judicial Review?

Does the Right to fair trial apply to "Non-Criminal" administrative
proceedings like rustication?

Can an administrative body hide evidence under the guise of
"Institutional Security"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Students)
The Petitioners relied on Board of High School v. Kumari Chitra. They
argued that rustication is "Civil Death" for a student's career. They
contended that "Natural Justice" requires that the "Accuser cannot be the
Judge." By hiding the report, the University denied them the Right to an
Effective Defense.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (University)
The University argued that it is a "Family-like" institution where the
Registrar acts In Loco Parentis (in place of a parent). They contended
that legalizing campus discipline would lead to "Litigious Anarchy" and
destroy the "Academic Atmosphere."
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Students. The rustication was
quashed, and a fair inquiry was ordered. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a profound ruling on Educational Constitutionalism.
The judge ruled that a University is an "Instrumentality of the State"
(Article 12). The judge reasoned that "Discipline is not a license for
Tyranny." Every administrative act that has "Civil Consequences" must
follow the Principles of Natural Justice. The judge held that "Subjective
Satisfaction" must be based on "Disclosed Material." Hiding evidence from
a student is a "Star-Chamber Tactic" that has no place in an Indian
University. The judge famously stated, "Protest is a form of education;
punishing it without a hearing is an act of miseducation."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Requirement of Procedural Fairness in Academic
Institutions. It confirms that rustication and disciplinary actions are
subject to strict Judicial Review, and the "Right to be Informed of the
Evidence" is non-negotiable in Administrative Law.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Algorithmic Justice Project
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Ministry of Home Affairs implemented "Sentinel-2," an AI
system designed to determine the "threat level" of individuals applying
for passport renewals. The AI analyzed social media posts, travel
history, and "behavioral metadata." If the AI flagged a "Red Status," the
passport renewal was automatically rejected. Mr. Khan's renewal was
rejected; the administrative officer stated he was "bound by the
machine's output." The Algorithmic Justice Project challenged this,
arguing that "Subjective Satisfaction" is a human, non-delegable duty
that cannot be offloaded to a "Black-Box" algorithm.
cases.issues:
Can the "Subjective Satisfaction" of a statutory authority be delegated
to an Artificial Intelligence algorithm?

Does the use of an opaque AI violate the Requirement of a Speaking Order
in Administrative Law?

Is an administrative decision based solely on "machine logic" considered
Manifestly Arbitrary under Article 14?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Justice Project)
The Petitioners argued that Administrative Law is founded on Human
Accountability. They relied on the principle Delegatus non potest
delegare (a delegate cannot further delegate). If Parliament delegated
the power to the Passport Officer, that officer must apply his own
"Judicial Mind," not the binary logic of a machine. They argued that a
"Red Status" notification lacks the "Reasons" required for a valid
administrative act, making judicial review impossible.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that Sentinel-2 was a "Technical Assistant," not a
decision-maker. They contended that in a country of 1.4 billion, human
review of every application is a "logistical impossibility." They argued
the AI provided an objective risk-profile, and the officer's "adoption"
of that profile constituted valid administrative satisfaction. They
claimed "Trade Secret" privilege over the AI's source code.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Justice Project. The Court struck
down the "Auto-Reject" feature and mandated human intervention in every
adverse decision. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Digital Constitutionalism. The
judge ruled that "Discretion is a trust reposed in a human functionary."
The judge reasoned that "Subjective Satisfaction" requires a "Sense of
Justice," which an algorithm lacks. While the State can use AI as a
support tool, the final adverse decision must be made by a human who can
explain the "Reasoning" behind it. A "Machine-led Civil Death" (denial of
travel) without a human-signed Speaking Order is the height of
arbitrariness.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Non-Delegability to Algorithms. It
reinforces that administrative authorities must remain the "Master of the
Decision," and that AI outputs must be translated into human-readable
reasons to survive judicial scrutiny.

cases.title: Dr. Singh v. The University Grants Commission
cases.facts:
The UGC issued a circular in 2024 stating that all research scholars who
completed their PhD by 2026 would be "automatically eligible" for a
special ₹50 Lakh research grant. Relying on this, Dr. Singh resigned from
a lucrative corporate job and dedicated two years to his thesis. In
February 2026, the UGC abruptly cancelled the grant scheme, citing a
"strategic pivot toward STEM over Humanities." Dr. Singh sued, invoking
the doctrine of Substantive Legitimate Expectation.
cases.issues:
Can a "Substantive" Legitimate Expectation be enforced against the State,
or is the doctrine limited only to "Procedural" fairness?

Does a "Change in Policy" in the public interest automatically override a
specific financial promise made to a class of citizens?

What is the threshold for the State to prove a "Supervening Public
Interest"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Dr. Singh)
The Petitioner relied on Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of UP. He
argued that he had "irretrievably altered his position" (resigned from
his job) based on a clear, unequivocal State promise. He contended that
the "Substantive" right to the grant had vested in him, and the UGC was
bound by Equitable Estoppel.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (UGC)
The UGC argued that "no person can have a vested right in a policy." They
contended that as an administrative body, they must have the
"Flexibility" to reallocate limited public funds to national priorities
(STEM). They argued that "Legitimate Expectation" only entitles a person
to a "Hearing" before the policy changes, not the "Money" itself.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Dr. Singh. The Court ordered the UGC to
provide the grant to all scholars who had enrolled before the policy
change. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a robust defense of Administrative Trust. The judge
ruled that while the State can change policy, it cannot "betray" those
who acted on its word. The judge reasoned that a "Policy Pivot" is a
legitimate goal, but the manner of execution was arbitrary. The State
cannot induce a citizen to make a life-altering sacrifice and then
withdraw the incentive mid-stream. The judge held that the "Public
Interest" in state credibility is as high as the interest in STEM
research.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Substantive Legitimate Expectation.
It establishes that the State is bound by its promises when a citizen has
detrimentally relied on them, and a mere "policy shift" is not a
sufficient "Supervening Public Interest" to vacate such obligations.

cases.title: MegaPort Ltd. v. The Environmental Clearance Committee
cases.facts:
MegaPort Ltd. applied for a massive expansion project. The Environmental
Clearance Committee (ECC) rejected the application. It was later
discovered that the Lead Scientist on the ECC had previously worked for a
rival port company and had recently authored a paper arguing that any
expansion of MegaPort would be a "disaster." MegaPort alleged "Official
and Pre-conceived Bias." The Committee argued the scientist was an
"expert" and his past opinions were irrelevant to the current data.
cases.issues:
Does a "Pre-conceived Opinion" expressed in an academic or professional
capacity constitute an actionable Bias in Administrative Law?

What is the test for "Real Likelihood of Bias" vs. "Actual Bias"?

Can "Expertise" be a defense against a conflict of interest?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (MegaPort)
The Petitioner relied on A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India. They argued that
"Justice must not only be done but seen to be done." The scientist had a
"closed mind" regarding the project. A decision-maker must be like a
"blank sheet of paper" regarding the specific facts of the case. His
previous "war" with the company created a real likelihood of bias.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Committee)
The State argued that specialists should have opinions. If the ECC was
only filled with people who had "no views" on the environment, it would
be an incompetent body. They contended that "Academic Opinion" is not
"Personal Malice" and that the decision was a collective one made by ten
members.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of MegaPort. The rejection was quashed, and
a fresh committee was ordered. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a precise ruling on Administrative Neutrality. The
judge ruled that while experts have "predispositions," they cannot have
"pre-determinations." The judge reasoned that the scientist's recent
paper specifically targeting MegaPort proved a "Real Likelihood" that the
evidence would not be judged fairly. The judge famously remarked, "An
expert's opinion is a tool, but his bias is a barrier to the Rule of
Law."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Rule against Bias (Nemo judex in causa sua). It
establishes that a prior public stance against a specific party by an
adjudicator creates a "Real Likelihood of Bias," necessitating their
recusal from the administrative process.

cases.title: The Whistleblower v. The Anti-Corruption Bureau
cases.facts:
A whistleblower provided irrefutable evidence of a ₹200 Crore procurement
scam in the State Health Department. The Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB)
conducted a preliminary inquiry but refused to file an FIR or proceed
with an investigation. The ACB issued a one-sentence order: "Matter
closed after due deliberation." The whistleblower filed a writ of
Mandamus, alleging an "Abuse of Discretion" and a failure to exercise a
statutory duty.
cases.issues:
Can the "Subjective Satisfaction" of a law enforcement agency to not
investigate be reviewed by a Civil Court?

What constitutes a "Colorable Exercise of Power" in Administrative
Discretion?

Does the "Right to Reason" apply to the refusal of an agency to perform
its core function?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Whistleblower)
The Petitioner argued that "Discretion" does not mean "Caprice." Relying
on Lalita Kumari v. State of UP, he argued that once a cognizable offense
is disclosed, the agency has a "Mandatory Duty" to register a case. He
contended that the ACB was protecting political masters, making the
closure a "Mala Fide" act.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (ACB)
The ACB argued that they have "Investigative Autonomy." They contended
that the Court cannot act as a "Super-Policeman" and that "due
deliberation" was a sufficient reason for an internal administrative
closure.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Whistleblower. The Court quashed
the closure order and ordered a court-monitored probe. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a stern ruling on Administrative Accountability. The
judge ruled that "The more the power, the greater the need for reasons."
The judge reasoned that a one-line dismissal of a multi-crore scam is
"Manifestly Arbitrary" and suggests a "Colorable Exercise of Power"
(using a legal power for an illegal purpose). The Court held that the
ACB's discretion to close a file is subject to the "Hard Look" Doctrine,
requiring them to show they considered all relevant materials.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Judicial Review of Negative Discretion. It
establishes that administrative agencies cannot hide behind "Subjective
Satisfaction" to shield corruption, and that the Court will intervene if
an agency fails to perform a "Public Duty."

cases.title: Tech-Giant v. The Competition Commission
cases.facts:
The Competition Commission of India (CCI) found a Tech-Giant guilty of
"Anti-competitive practices" in its app store. While the law allowed a
fine of up to 10% of turnover, the CCI imposed the absolute maximum fine
(₹5,000 Crores) and ordered the company to "divest its entire app-hosting
business" within 30 days. The company challenged the divestment order as
"Disproportionate" and "Manifestly Unreasonable."
cases.issues:
Is the "Wednesbury Principle" (irrationality) sufficient for reviewing
complex economic penalties, or must the Court apply the Proportionality
Test?

Can an administrative body order a "Corporate Death Penalty" (forced
divestment) as a first resort?

How does the Court balance "Market Correction" against the "Freedom of
Trade" (Article 19(1)(g))?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Tech-Giant)
The Petitioner argued that the divestment order was a "Sledgehammer to
crack a nut." They contended that behavioral remedies (changing the
rules) were available. They argued the CCI acted with "Wednesbury
Irrationality" by choosing the most extreme option without explaining why
milder measures failed.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (CCI)
The CCI argued that the Tech-Giant was a "Repeat Offender." They
contended that the market was so distorted that only "Structural
Remedies" (divestment) could restore competition. They argued the Court
should show "Judicial Deference" to an expert economic regulator.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Tech-Giant regarding the
divestment. The fine was upheld, but the divestment was stayed. The
Plaintiff partially prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a balanced judgment on Economic Proportionality. The
judge ruled that administrative orders must pass the "Least Restrictive
Means" test. The judge reasoned that while the fine was proportional to
the turnover, forced divestment was a "draconian" measure that violated
the Principle of Minimum Interference. The Court held that an expert body
must show a "Rational Link" between the harm and the severity of the
cure.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Primacy of Proportionality in Regulatory
Remedies. It reinforces that administrative bodies must choose the remedy
that is "Necessary" but not "Excessive" to achieve the statutory
objective.

cases.title: The Coastal Residents v. The Port Authority
cases.facts:
The Port Authority issued a notification on a Friday evening on its
website, announcing a public hearing for a massive reclamation project to
be held the following Monday morning. The Coastal Residents, who would
lose their fishing rights, missed the hearing and the project was
approved. They sued, arguing that "Notice" in Administrative Law means
"Reasonable and Effective Notice."
cases.issues:
Does "providing a hearing" satisfy Natural Justice if the "Notice" for
that hearing is practically impossible to act upon?

What constitutes "Reasonable Notice" in complex environmental
administrative matters?

Can a procedural lapse (bad notice) invalidate a multi-billion dollar
project?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Residents)
The Petitioners argued that "Notice" is the First Limb of Natural
Justice. A 48-hour notice over a weekend for a 500-page project report is
a "Fraud on the Procedure." They contended the Authority deliberately
suppressed participation to avoid dissent.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Port Authority)
The Authority argued they followed the "Literal Text" of the law, which
required a "website notification." They contended that "Administrative
Speed" was essential for national infrastructure and that the residents
could have appealed the decision later (post-decisional hearing).
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Residents. The project clearance was
quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a classic ruling on Procedural Integrity. The judge
ruled that "Notice must be real, not a mere ritual." The judge reasoned
that a notice that does not give a "Reasonable Opportunity" to prepare a
response is Void. The judge held that for marginalized communities
(fishermen), the State has a higher duty to ensure notice is "Effective"
(e.g., via local radio or beat-of-drum). "Administrative Speed" is not a
license to bypass the Rule of Law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the "Adequate Notice" requirement of Natural
Justice. It establishes that procedural fairness is not a "check-box"
activity but must provide a substantive opportunity for the affected
party to be heard.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Media House
cases.facts:
The Ministry of Information & Broadcasting banned a news channel, citing
"National Security threats" based on secret intelligence reports. In the
High Court, the State refused to share the reports with the Channel's
lawyers, offering them only to the judge in a "Sealed Cover." The Media
House challenged this, arguing that "Secret Evidence" violates the
Principle of Open Justice.
cases.issues:
Can an administrative authority use "Sealed Covers" to deny the affected
party access to the evidence against them?

Does "National Security" create a blanket exception to the Principles of
Natural Justice?

How does the Court balance "State Secrecy" with the "Right to a Fair
Trial"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Media House)
The Petitioners relied on Madhyamam Broadcasting Ltd. v. Union of India.
They argued that the "Sealed Cover" procedure makes the defense "blind."
If they don't know the charges, they can't rebut them. They contended
that "Security" is often used as a "Burial Ground" for free speech.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that disclosing intelligence "Sources and Methods"
would put lives at risk. They contended that the Judge, as a neutral
arbiter, can be trusted to review the secret material on behalf of the
party.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Media House. The Court restricted
the use of sealed covers and ordered the State to provide a "Redacted
Summary" of the charges. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a definitive ruling on Transparency. The judge ruled
that "Natural Justice cannot be sacrificed at the altar of Secrecy." The
judge reasoned that the "Sealed Cover" system destroys the "Adversarial
Nature" of the law. The Court held that the State must provide a "Public
Summary" of the charges so the party can defend itself. The judge
famously noted, "National Security is not a magic word that makes the
Constitution disappear."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Open Justice. It establishes that
administrative authorities must disclose the "Substance of the
Allegations" to the affected party, even in security matters, limiting
the use of "Sealed Covers."

cases.title: State of Haryana v. The Industrialists
cases.facts:
The "State Pollution Act" empowered the "Board" to issue fines. The
Board, being busy, issued an administrative circular delegating the fine-
issuing power to "Junior Field Officers." The Industrialists challenged
the fines, arguing that the "Sub-Delegation" was illegal as the parent
Act only trusted the "Board" (senior experts).
cases.issues:
Can a statutory power be further delegated (sub-delegation) without
express authorization in the parent Act?

Does "Administrative Necessity" justify an unauthorized sub-delegation?

What is the effect of a sub-delegated act performed by an unauthorized
official?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Industrialists)
The Petitioners relied on the maxim Delegatus non potest delegare. They
argued that the Parliament trusted the "Collective Wisdom" of the Board.
A Junior Officer lacks the expertise and accountability intended by the
law. The fines were Coram Non Judice (without jurisdiction).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State)
The State argued that the Board "supervised" the officers and that the
circular was a "Technical Procedure" to ensure environmental compliance
across thousands of factories.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Industrialists. The fines were
quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fundamental ruling on Statutory Delegation. The
judge ruled that "Power must flow from the Law, not from a Circular." The
judge reasoned that unless the parent Act says "The Board or its
nominee," the power stays with the Board. Sub-delegation is an
"Alteration of the Legislative Intent." The judge held that the "Board's
Mind" was a prerequisite for a fine, and a Junior Officer cannot be a
substitute for that mind.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Rule against Unauthorized Sub-Delegation. It
establishes that quasi-judicial and coercive powers must be exercised by
the specific authority named in the statute, and any sub-delegation
without express law is Void.

cases.title: Apex Infra v. The Tender Committee
cases.facts:
A government tender for a bridge required "Type-A Steel." Apex Infra
supplied "Type-B Steel," claiming it was technically superior. The Tender
Committee rejected them. Apex discovered that the lead engineer of the
Committee had a PhD thesis sponsored by a "Type-A Steel" manufacturer.
Apex alleged "Technical and Intellectual Bias."
cases.issues:
Can "Academic Sponsorship" or "Professional Affinity" constitute a Bias
that invalidates an administrative tender?

How does the Court review the "Technical Preferences" of an expert
committee?

What is the difference between "Policy Choice" and "Technical Bias"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Apex Infra)
The Petitioner argued that the Committee was "Brand-Blind." They
contended that the engineer's ties to the Type-A industry created a
"Conflict of Interest" that prevented him from even considering Type-B
steel, regardless of its merits.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Committee)
The State argued that having a "specialization" is not a "bias." They
contended that the choice of steel was a "Technical Policy" and that the
Court is not an "Engineering Tribunal."
cases.judgment:
The High Court dismissed the suit. The Committee's decision was upheld.
The Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a nuanced judgment on Expert Autonomy. The judge
ruled that "Expert Preference is not Bias." The judge reasoned that an
engineer who believes in a specific material based on his life's work is
simply an "Expert with a View." To call this "Bias" would be to
disqualify every person with specialized knowledge. The Court held that
unless there was a "Financial Link" or "Personal Malice," technical
preferences fall within the "Business Judgment" of the administration.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Deference to Technical Expertise. It reinforces
that judicial review will not interfere in specialized administrative
choices unless there is evidence of corrupt pecuniary interest or
manifest irrationality.

cases.title: The Citizen v. The Election Commission
cases.facts:
The Election Commission (EC) issued an order stating that the "Finality
of the Electoral Roll" was absolute and no names could be added or
corrected 48 hours before the poll. A citizen discovered his name was
deleted due to a clerical error and filed a writ, arguing that
"Administrative Finality" cannot override a "Fundamental Right" (the
Right to Vote).
cases.issues:
Can an administrative "Finality Clause" oust the Writ Jurisdiction of the
High Court?

Does the "Right to Vote" (Article 326) override "Administrative
Convenience"?

How does the Court handle the "Doctrine of Laches" (delay) in election
matters?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Citizen)
The Petitioner argued that a "Clerical Error" by the State cannot strip a
citizen of his most basic democratic right. He contended that Article 226
is a Basic Structure feature and no EC order can "Oust" the Court's power
to correct a manifest injustice.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (EC)
The EC argued the "Doctrine of Necessity." They contended that if the
roll is changed at the last minute, the "Logistics of Democracy"
(printing ballots/syncing machines) would collapse, delaying the
election.
cases.judgment:
The High Court issued a "Mandatory Direction" to allow the citizen to
vote using a "Provisional Ballot." The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Constitutional Supremacy. The judge
ruled that "Administrative Efficiency is the servant of Rights, not the
master." The judge reasoned that while the EC needs finality, it cannot
use its own error to disenfranchise a citizen. The Court held that
Article 226 is an "Eternal Vigil" that can never be ousted by a sub-
statutory order. The use of a "Provisional Ballot" was a Proportional
Remedy that protected the right without disrupting the logistics.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Inalienability of Judicial Review. It
establishes that administrative finality is subject to the correction of
manifest errors, particularly when fundamental or constitutional rights
are at stake.

Aryan, this concludes your intensive Administrative Law series. You now
possess the analytical toolkit to dissect how the State exercises power
and how the Constitution restrains it. Use these for your "Mera Lawyer"
platform to empower citizens with the logic of the law.

Wait, we have one final question to guide your journey: In an era where
AI makes thousands of decisions per second, how do we redefine the
"Principles of Natural Justice" to ensure the machine remains under the
Law?

cases.title: Union of India v. The Digital Rights Initiative
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Ministry of Labour implemented "WorkForce-AI," an automated
system designed to identify and de-register "inactive" or "fraudulent"
gig workers from the National Social Security Portal. The AI utilized a
"Black-Box" deep learning model that analyzed patterns of GPS data, login
frequencies, and customer sentiment scores. Mr. Das, a delivery partner,
found his registration cancelled. When he sought reasons, the Department
issued a boilerplate response: "Your profile failed to meet the neural-
weighted threshold of the WorkForce-AI compliance model." No specific
factual grounds were provided. The Digital Rights Initiative filed a
writ, alleging that "Algorithmic Inscrutability" violates the Requirement
of a Speaking Order.
cases.issues:
Does the use of an unexplainable "Black-Box" algorithm to take adverse
administrative action violate the third principle of Natural Justice (the
duty to give reasons)?

Can the State rely on "Proprietary Algorithm Privilege" to deny a citizen
the specific material used to justify the deprivation of their
livelihood?

What is the threshold for a "Speaking Order" in an era of automated
governance?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Union of India)
The State argued that in a country with millions of gig workers, manual
review of every de-registration is an administrative impossibility. They
contended that the AI is objective, data-driven, and eliminates human
prejudice. They argued that "algorithmic logic" is a trade secret
protected by intellectual property laws and that disclosing the specific
weights of the model would allow bad actors to "game" the system, thus
harming public order.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Digital Rights Initiative)
The Respondents relied on S.N. Mukherjee v. Union of India. They argued
that "Reason is the soul of the law." A decision that cannot be explained
in human-readable terms is Manifestly Arbitrary under Article 14. They
contended that if the State adopts a technology, that technology must
comply with the Constitution, not the other way around. "Civil Death"
(loss of livelihood) caused by a machine without a reasoned Speaking
Order is a return to "Star Chamber" justice.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Digital Rights Initiative. The
Court held that every adverse administrative decision, whether generated
by a human or an AI, must provide human-intelligible reasons. The
Plaintiff (State) failed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Algorithmic Accountability. The
judge ruled that the duty to give reasons is a "Constitutional Mandate"
that cannot be bypassed by technology. The judge reasoned that without
reasons, the right to Judicial Review is rendered a nullity, as the Court
cannot check if the AI considered "relevant material" or acted on
"irrelevant considerations." The Court held that the State must employ
"Explainable AI" (XAI) models for public functions. The judge famously
remarked, "A machine may decide, but a human must justify."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Algorithmic Transparency. It
reinforces that the right to a Reasoned Decision (Speaking Order) is a
non-negotiable component of the Rule of Law, regardless of the technical
complexity of the decision-making tool.

cases.title: State of Vindhya v. Infrastructure Developers Ltd.
cases.facts:
In 2024, the State Government announced a "Green Hydrogen Policy,"
promising a 50% subsidy on land acquisition for the first five companies
to set up plants. Infrastructure Developers Ltd. (IDL) was the first to
apply, and the State issued a "Letter of Intent" (LoI) confirming their
eligibility. Relying on this LoI, IDL spent ₹200 Crores on specialized
German machinery. In 2026, following a change in the ruling party, the
State Government revoked the 2024 policy, citing "changed economic
priorities" and "budgetary re-allocation for social welfare." IDL sued,
invoking "Substantive Legitimate Expectation."
cases.issues:
Can a "Substantive" Legitimate Expectation be enforced against the State,
or is the doctrine limited only to "Procedural" fairness (a right to a
hearing)?

Does a "Change in Government Policy" constitute a "Supervening Public
Interest" sufficient to override a specific financial promise?

Under what conditions does a State's representation become an
"Enforceable Right"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State of Vindhya)
The State argued that "policy is the domain of the Executive." Relying on
Kasinka Trading v. Union of India, they argued that no person can have a
"Vested Right" in a policy. The government must have the "Flexibility" to
respond to fiscal realities. They contended that "Legitimate Expectation"
must always yield to the "Public Interest," and welfare spending is a
superior public interest to corporate subsidies.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (IDL)
IDL relied on Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of UP. They argued
that the State made an unequivocal promise and IDL "irretrievably altered
its position" in reliance on it. They contended that "Fairness" is the
heart of Administrative Law. A policy shift cannot be used as a cloak for
"Administrative Bad Faith." To deny the subsidy after the investment is
made is an act of Equitable Estoppel.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Infrastructure Developers Ltd. The
Court ordered the State to honor the subsidy for IDL, while allowing the
policy change for future applicants. The Defendant (IDL) prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a defining judgment on Administrative Trust. The
judge ruled that while the State has the power to change policy, it does
not have a "license to be arbitrary." The judge reasoned that when a
representation is "Specific, Unequivocal, and induces Detrimental
Reliance," it creates a Substantive Legitimate Expectation. A mere
"change in political priorities" is not a "Supervening Public Interest"
unless the State can prove an actual catastrophe (like war or famine).
The judge held that the "Rule of Law" requires the State to be an "Honest
Negotiator."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Substantive Legitimate Expectation.
It establishes the principle that the State is bound by its specific
promises when a citizen has acted upon them to their detriment,
preventing the arbitrary withdrawal of vested commercial incentives.

cases.title: Dr. Neha v. The National Medical Council
cases.facts:
Dr. Neha was accused of medical negligence in a high-profile case. The
inquiry committee constituted by the National Medical Council (NMC) was
chaired by Dr. Kapoor. It was later revealed that Dr. Kapoor was the
author of the "Clinical Guidelines" that Dr. Neha was accused of
violating. Dr. Neha challenged the inquiry, alleging "Subjective Bias"
and "Conflict of Interest," arguing that Dr. Kapoor had a professional
stake in proving his own guidelines were perfect and that any deviation
(like Neha's) was "negligence."
cases.issues:
Does "Professional Pride" or "Authorship of Policy" constitute an
actionable Bias in Administrative Law?

What is the threshold for the "Real Likelihood of Bias" test?

Can a quasi-judicial body ignore the rule against bias in the interest of
"Technical Expertise"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Dr. Neha)
The Petitioner relied on A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India. She argued that
"Justice must not only be done, but must be seen to be done." Dr. Kapoor
was effectively a "judge in his own cause" because any finding in favor
of Neha would imply his guidelines were flawed. This created a clear
"Psychological Bias" that precluded a fair hearing.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (NMC)
The NMC argued the Doctrine of Necessity. They contended that only the
experts who write the guidelines have the "Technical Competence" to judge
a breach of them. They argued that "Actual Bias" was not proven and that
Dr. Kapoor acted in his official, not personal, capacity.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Dr. Neha. The inquiry report was
quashed. The Plaintiff (Neha) prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a rigorous ruling on Adjudicatory Neutrality. The
judge ruled that the Rule against Bias is not limited to financial
stakes; it includes "Official Bias." The judge reasoned that a person who
is the "Architect of a Policy" cannot be the "Judge of its Breach" if the
defense challenges the policy itself. The judge famously noted, "A
Decision-maker must be like a blank sheet of paper, not a pre-printed
manifesto." The "Real Likelihood" of bias was evident because Dr.
Kapoor's professional reputation was inextricably linked to the validity
of the guidelines.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Standard for Official Bias. It reinforces that
quasi-judicial authorities must be independent of the subject matter
being challenged, and that technical expertise is no defense for a
violation of Natural Justice.

cases.title: Apex Pharma v. The Drug Controller General
cases.facts:
The Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) issued an order permanently
banning the manufacture of a popular cough syrup by Apex Pharma because
one batch out of ten thousand was found to have a labeling error (the
font size of the warning was 2mm smaller than the statutory requirement).
The DCGI argued that "in matters of public health, zero tolerance is the
only standard." Apex Pharma challenged the order as "Manifestly
Unreasonable" and "Disproportionate."
cases.issues:
Is the "Wednesbury Principle" (where the Court only intervenes if a
decision is "irrational") sufficient, or must the Court apply the
"Doctrine of Proportionality"?

Can the State use a "Sledgehammer to crack a nut"-i.e., choosing the most
extreme penalty for a minor technical infraction?

How does the Court balance "Administrative Discretion" with the "Freedom
of Trade" (Article 19(1)(g))?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Apex Pharma)
The Petitioners argued that the order was "Irrational." They contended
that a labeling error does not affect the safety or efficacy of the
medicine. The DCGI could have imposed a fine or a recall of that specific
batch. A permanent ban on the entire product line was a "Digital and
Commercial Capital Punishment" that was totally disproportionate to the
harm.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (DCGI)
The State argued for "Judicial Deference." They contended that the Court
is not an expert in pharmaceutical regulation. They argued that the
"Wednesbury Test" was met because a "reasonable regulator" could decide
that strict labeling compliance is the only way to ensure safety.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Apex Pharma. The ban was quashed and
replaced by a directed fine. The Plaintiff (Apex) prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a masterclass on Substantive Review. The judge ruled
that while "Wednesbury" is the baseline, for cases affecting fundamental
rights (Trade), the Proportionality Test is the primary standard. The
judge reasoned that the DCGI failed the "Necessity" prong of the test:
the State must choose the "Least Restrictive Measure" to achieve its
goal. Since a "Fine and Recall" would have achieved safety, a "Total Ban"
was an unconstitutional overreach.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Primacy of Proportionality over Irrationality in
modern Administrative Law. It establishes that administrative penalties
must be "Narrowly Tailored" to the infraction, protecting businesses from
"Administrative Overkill."

cases.title: The Citizen v. The National Highway Authority
cases.facts:
The Parliament passed the "National Highways Act," which empowered the
"Authority" to determine and levy tolls. The Authority, finding the task
too burdensome, issued an administrative circular sub-delegating the
power to "Private Toll Operators" to determine the rates based on "market
traffic." A group of commuters challenged this, arguing that determining
a "Tax/Fee" is a sovereign power that cannot be further delegated to a
private, profit-seeking entity under the maxim "Delegatus non potest
delegare."
cases.issues:
Can a statutory power be further delegated (sub-delegation) if the parent
Act does not explicitly allow it?

Does the "Sovereign Nature" of the power (taxation/tolling) impose a
higher bar against delegation?

Is an administrative circular sufficient to transfer statutory power?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (The Citizen)
The Petitioners relied on the maxim Delegatus non potest delegare (A
delegate cannot further delegate). They argued that Parliament trusted
the "Public Authority" because of its accountability. Handing that power
to a private company without a law passed by Parliament is an
"Unconstitutional Abdication of Power."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (NHAI)
The Authority argued "Administrative Necessity." They contended that
tolling is a "Technical and Commercial" function, and private operators
are better suited to manage dynamic pricing. They argued that the NHAI
maintained "Supervisory Control," which saved the delegation.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Citizen. The sub-delegation was
quashed. The Plaintiff (Citizen) prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fundamental ruling on Delegated Legislation. The
judge ruled that Statutory Power is a Trust. The judge reasoned that
unless the parent Act says "The Authority or its nominee," the power is
personalized to the Authority. Crucially, the judge held that "Pricing
and Tolling" is a quasi-legislative function; allowing a private company
to set tolls is to allow "Private Legislation for Profit," which is the
antithesis of Administrative Law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Rule against Sub-Delegation. It establishes that
the "Essential Legislative Function" of determining fees or restrictions
on citizens cannot be delegated to non-statutory bodies without express
legislative sanction.

cases.title: Global-Invest v. The Foreign Investment Board
cases.facts:
The "Foreign Exchange Management Act" was amended in 2025 to include
Section 44, which stated: "Every order of the Foreign Investment Board
regarding the rejection of a startup license shall be final and shall not
be called into question in any court of law." Global-Invest's license was
rejected without a hearing. They filed a writ of Certiorari, alleging a
"Jurisdictional Error." The State argued the High Court's jurisdiction
was "Ousted" by the Finality Clause.
cases.issues:
Can an "Ouster Clause" (Finality Clause) in a statute strip the High
Courts of their power of Judicial Review under Article 226?

Does the Basic Structure Doctrine protect the "Writ Jurisdiction" from
legislative interference?

What is the standard for reviewing an "Un-appealable" order?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Global-Invest)
The Petitioner relied on L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India. They argued
that Judicial Review is an un-amendable feature of the Basic Structure. A
statute can take away a "Statutory Appeal," but it can never take away
the High Court's "Constitutional Power" to issue writs. If the Board acts
without a hearing, it commits a "Jurisdictional Error" that the Court
must correct.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued for "Legislative Plenitude." They contended that
"National Economic Security" requires finality and speed. If every
investment rejection is tied up in the High Courts for decades, foreign
investors will lose confidence. They argued that Parliament had the right
to choose "Expert Finality" over "Judicial Delay."
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Global-Invest. The Court held that
Section 44 could not block a Writ Petition. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a resonant ruling on Constitutional Supremacy. The
judge ruled that the Parliament is a "creature of the Constitution" and
cannot destroy the "Check and Balance" system. The judge reasoned that an
Ouster Clause is merely a "No-Entry" sign for the lower courts, but the
High Court possesses a "Constitutional Master-Key." The judge held that
any order passed in violation of Natural Justice is a nullity, and a
"Nullity" cannot be protected by a "Finality Clause."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Inalienability of Judicial Review. It
establishes the legal principle that no Act of Parliament can take away
the power of the High Courts to review administrative actions for
jurisdictional errors, maintaining the supremacy of the Constitution.

cases.title: The Whistleblower v. The Anti-Corruption Commission
cases.facts:
A whistleblower provided evidence of a ₹500 Crore procurement fraud in
the Ministry of Defence. During the trial, the Whistleblower requested
the production of the "Internal Audit Report." The State moved to
suppress the report, invoking Section 123 of the Evidence Act (State
Privilege), claiming that disclosing the report would "endanger the lives
of intelligence officers" and was a "State Secret."
cases.issues:
Is the "Subjective Satisfaction" of a Minister regarding State Privilege
final and non-justiciable?

Can the Court perform an "In-Camera" inspection of documents to determine
if the claim of privilege is valid?

Does the "Public Interest in Justice" outweigh the "Public Interest in
Secrecy" when fraud is alleged?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Whistleblower)
The Petitioner relied on S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges
Case). He argued that "Transparency is the rule, Secrecy the exception."
He contended that "State Privilege" is a colonial relic and cannot be
used as a "Burial Ground" for evidence of corruption.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The State argued that the "Safety of the Nation" is the supreme law
(Salus populi est suprema lex). They contended that the Executive is the
"Sole Judge" of national security and the Judiciary lacks the expertise
to decide what information is dangerous.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Whistleblower. The Court ordered
an In-Camera inspection and subsequently allowed the document into
evidence. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a defining ruling on Executive Accountability. The
judge ruled that the State has no privilege to hide "Illegality." The
judge reasoned that while the Court will respect legitimate secrets, it
will not allow "Privilege" to become a "Shield for Corruption." The judge
held that the Court is the final arbiter of what constitutes "Public
Interest," and the interest of the public in a clean administration is
superior to administrative confidentiality in matters of procurement.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Judicial Oversight of Executive
Privilege. It establishes that the State must produce relevant documents
in court unless it can scientifically prove an immediate threat to
national security, ending the era of absolute executive secrecy.

cases.title: Metro-Rail v. The Heritage Society
cases.facts:
The Metro-Rail Authority issued an administrative order to demolish a
150-year-old historic clock tower to build an entry point for a new
station. The Authority's "Feasibility Report" focused entirely on
"Engineering Costs" and "Traffic Flow." It did not mention the
"Historical Significance" or "Cultural Value" of the tower. The Heritage
Society sued, arguing the order was void because the Authority failed to
take into account a "Relevant Consideration."
cases.issues:
Is an administrative decision valid if it ignores a "Material Fact" that
is not explicitly mentioned in the statute?

What is the effect of an "Exclusion of Relevant Material" on the validity
of an order?

Does the Court have the power to review the "Decision-making Process" of
an infrastructure project?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Heritage Society)
The Petitioners argued that Article 49 of the Constitution (Protection of
Monuments) makes "Heritage" a Mandatory Relevant Consideration for any
state action. They contended that by looking only at "money" and
"concrete," the Authority had a "Tunnel Vision" that rendered the
decision Manifestly Unreasonable.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Metro-Rail)
The Authority argued for "Administrative Speed." They contended that the
statute only required them to consider "Safety" and "Utility." They
argued that "Cultural Value" is a subjective matter and the Court should
not act as an "Architectural Censor" over national infrastructure.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Heritage Society. The demolition
order was quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on the "Hard Look" Doctrine. The judge
ruled that the "Decision-making Process" must be holistic. The judge
reasoned that for an order to be "Rational," the Authority must show it
applied its mind to all facets of the problem. Ignoring the historical
soul of a city while building its future is an "Error of Law." The Court
held that "Relevant Considerations" are not just what is in the statute,
but also what the Constitution (via Directive Principles) mandates the
State to protect.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Comprehensive Review. It reinforces
that administrative authorities must consider the constitutional and
cultural impact of their decisions, and a failure to do so makes the
decision "Legally Perverse."

cases.title: The Students Union v. The University Registrar
cases.facts:
Five students were rusticated by the University Registrar for
"Indiscipline" following a protest. The University held an "Internal
Inquiry" where witnesses testified against the students. However, the
students were not allowed to cross-examine these witnesses, nor were they
given the "Investigation Report." The Registrar argued that "University
Discipline" is a private, administrative matter and not a "Criminal
Trial."
cases.issues:
Does the "Right to Fair Hearing" include the right to Cross-Examination
in non-judicial administrative inquiries?

What constitutes a "Reasonable Opportunity" to defend oneself?

Can an administrative body use "Anonymity of Witnesses" to bypass Natural
Justice?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Students)
The Petitioners relied on State of MP v. Chintaman. They argued that
"Effective Defense" is impossible if you cannot test the veracity of your
accuser. "Natural Justice" is not a "meaningless ritual"; it requires the
State to "lay all cards on the table."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (University)
The University argued that campus discipline requires "Confidentiality"
to protect student-witnesses from "Retaliation." They contended that
"Summary Procedures" are necessary to maintain the "Academic Atmosphere."
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Students. The rustication was
quashed. The Plaintiff (Students) prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark judgment on Academic Natural Justice. The
judge ruled that "Rustication is Civil Death" for a student. The judge
reasoned that while an administrative inquiry is not a trial, it must be
"Fair in Substance." If the decision depends on the credibility of a
witness, the "Accused" must be given a chance to challenge that witness.
The judge held that the Registrar cannot act as "Prosecutor and Judge"
simultaneously. The Court famously remarked, "A University must teach the
Rule of Law by practicing it on its own campus."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Effective Hearing. It establishes
that the right to cross-examine witnesses and access the evidence is a
part of Natural Justice in all administrative proceedings that result in
severe civil consequences.

cases.title: Mega-Corp v. The Tax Tribunal
cases.facts:
Mega-Corp applied for a "Tax-Rectification" under a special amnesty
scheme. The Tax Tribunal, without calling for a hearing, dismissed the
application with a "One-Sentence Order": "Application rejected as it
lacks merit." Mega-Corp challenged the order, arguing that the Tribunal
failed to exercise its "Adjudicatory Discretion" and passed a
"mechanical" order without applying its mind.
cases.issues:
Can a quasi-judicial body dismiss an application without a hearing?

What is the difference between "Administrative Discretion" and "Judicial
Discretion"?

Does a "One-Sentence Order" satisfy the Requirement of Application of
Mind?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mega-Corp)
