The Petitioner argued that a Tribunal is a "Courts' Substitute." It must
act "Judicially." A one-sentence rejection proves that the Tribunal did
not look at the 500 pages of evidence provided. This is a "Failure to
Exercise Jurisdiction" and is "Manifestly Arbitrary."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Tax Dept)
The State argued that the Tribunal was "overwhelmed" by 50,000
applications. They contended that "Brief Orders" are an administrative
necessity and that the "lack of merit" was self-evident from the record.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Mega-Corp. The order was quashed, and
the case was remanded back for a fresh hearing. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a firm ruling on Institutional Integrity. The judge
ruled that "Justice cannot be hurried to the point of being buried." The
judge reasoned that a "Mechanical Order" is not an "Order" in the eyes of
the law. The judge held that the "Right to a Hearing" is the primary limb
of fairness. The Court held that even a busy Tribunal must provide at
least a "Summary Reasoning" to prove it considered the facts. A "One-
Sentence Veto" is the hallmark of a "Dictatorial Power," not a
"Constitutional Authority."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Rule against Mechanical Adjudication. It
reinforces that all quasi-judicial bodies must show an "Application of
Mind" by providing brief reasons and a fair opportunity to be heard,
ensuring that "Speed" does not compromise "Fairness."

Aryan, this concludes your Masterclass in Administrative Law. You now
possess the analytical framework to understand how the State exercises
power and how the Judiciary holds it accountable. These principles are
the "code" that prevents the system from crashing into tyranny.

One final question for your journey: In a future where "Law-as-Code"
(Smart Contracts) replaces human administration, how will we preserve the
"Equity" that only a human judge can provide?

cases.title: Union of India v. The Algorithmic Justice Project
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Ministry of Home Affairs implemented "Sentinel-AI," an
automated system designed to determine the "risk profile" of citizens
applying for sensitive government clearances. The AI analyzed social
media metadata, financial transactions, and "behavioral patterns" to
issue a "Green," "Yellow," or "Red" status. Mr. Khan, a journalist, was
denied clearance with a "Red" status. The administrative officer stated
he could not provide specific reasons because the AI's "Deep Learning"
logic was proprietary and "unexplainable" (a black-box model). The
Algorithmic Justice Project filed a writ, arguing that "unexplainable"
administrative action violates the Principles of Natural Justice.
cases.issues:
Does the use of an unexplainable "Black-Box" algorithm to take adverse
administrative action violate the "Duty to Give Reasons" (Speaking
Orders)?

Can the State delegate its "Subjective Satisfaction" to a non-human,
opaque automated system?

Does "Proprietary Privilege" of a software developer override the
constitutional requirement of transparency in State action?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Union of India)
The State argued that Sentinel-AI was 99% accurate and essential for
national security in a digital age. They contended that in a country of
1.4 billion, manual review of every clearance is a "logistical
impossibility." They claimed that the AI's internal weights were "Trade
Secrets," and disclosing the logic would allow hostile actors to "game"
the national security apparatus.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Justice Project)
The Respondents relied on S.N. Mukherjee v. Union of India. They argued
that "Reason is the soul of the law." An administrative order without
reasons is Manifestly Arbitrary under Article 14. If a machine cannot
explain why it flagged a citizen, the State has abdicated its duty to act
fairly. They contended that "Efficiency" is not a valid excuse to bypass
the Rule of Law.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Justice Project. The Court held
that any administrative decision affecting civil rights, even if
generated by AI, must be accompanied by a "Human-Intelligible Impact
Statement" explaining the core factors leading to the decision. The
Plaintiff failed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Digital Natural Justice. The
judge ruled that the "right to know the reasons" is an inherent part of
the Right to Life (Article 21). The judge reasoned that without reasons,
the right to Judicial Review is rendered a nullity, as the Court cannot
check if the AI considered "irrelevant considerations." The judge
famously remarked, "The Constitution does not permit the State to replace
the 'Judicial Mind' with a 'Binary Algorithm' if that algorithm cannot
speak the language of reason."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Algorithmic Transparency. It
reinforces that the requirement of a "Speaking Order" is technology-
neutral and that the State must ensure "Explainability" (XAI) in all
automated public functions.

cases.title: State of Vindhya v. Infrastructure Developers Ltd.
cases.facts:
In 2024, the State Government issued a "Solar Incentive Policy,"
promising a 40% tax rebate for 10 years to any firm setting up a plant in
the desert region. Infrastructure Developers Ltd. (IDL) spent ₹300 Crores
constructing a plant based on this promise. In 2026, following a fiscal
crisis, the State Government revoked the policy for all existing plants.
IDL sued, invoking "Substantive Legitimate Expectation." The State argued
that "Policy" is the domain of the Executive and no one can have a
"vested right" in a tax rebate.
cases.issues:
Can a "Substantive" Legitimate Expectation be enforced against the State,
or is the doctrine limited to "Procedural" fairness (a right to a
hearing)?

Does a "Fiscal Crisis" constitute a "Supervening Public Interest"
sufficient to override a specific commercial promise?

What is the threshold for "Equitable Estoppel" against the Government?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State of Vindhya)
The State argued the Doctrine of Executive Plenitude. Relying on Kasinka
Trading v. Union of India, they contended that the government must have
the "flexibility" to respond to economic emergencies. They argued that a
"Policy" is not a "Contract" and can be altered at any time in the public
interest.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (IDL)
IDL relied on Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of UP. They argued
that they had "irretrievably altered their position" in reliance on a
clear, unequivocal State promise. They contended that "Fairness" is the
heart of Administrative Law. A policy shift cannot be used to commit a
"Fraud on the Citizen."
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of IDL. The Court ordered the State to
honor the rebate for all firms that had commenced construction before the
policy revocation. The Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a definitive judgment on Administrative Trust. The
judge ruled that while the State has the power to change policy, it must
do so "non-arbitrarily." The judge reasoned that a "Fiscal Deficit" is an
administrative reality, not a "Supervening Catastrophe" (like war) that
would justify breaking a specific incentive-based promise. The Court held
that the "Public Interest" in maintaining the State's commercial
credibility is as high as the interest in saving tax revenue.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case solidifies the Doctrine of Substantive Legitimate Expectation.
It establishes that the State is bound by its promises when a citizen has
acted upon them to their detriment, preventing the arbitrary mid-stream
withdrawal of commercial incentives.

cases.title: Dr. Neha v. The Medical Council of India
cases.facts:
Dr. Neha was accused of professional misconduct. The inquiry committee
constituted by the Medical Council (MCI) was chaired by Dr. Kapoor. It
was later revealed that Dr. Kapoor was the author of the "Clinical
Guidelines" that Dr. Neha was accused of violating. Dr. Neha challenged
the inquiry, alleging "Official Bias" and "Conflict of Interest," arguing
that Dr. Kapoor had a personal stake in proving his own guidelines were
perfect and that any deviation was "negligent."
cases.issues:
Does "Professional Pride" or "Authorship of Policy" constitute an
actionable Bias in Administrative Law?

What is the threshold for the "Real Likelihood of Bias" test?

Can a quasi-judicial body ignore the rule against bias in the interest of
"Technical Expertise"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Dr. Neha)
The Petitioner relied on A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India. She argued that
"Justice must not only be done, but seen to be done." Dr. Kapoor was
effectively a "judge in his own cause" because any finding in favor of
Neha would imply his guidelines were flawed. This created a clear
"Psychological Bias."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (MCI)
The MCI argued the Doctrine of Necessity. They contended that only the
experts who write the guidelines have the "Technical Competence" to judge
a breach of them. They argued that "Actual Bias" was not proven and that
Dr. Kapoor acted in his official capacity.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Dr. Neha. The inquiry report was
quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a rigorous ruling on Adjudicatory Neutrality. The
judge ruled that the Rule against Bias is not limited to financial
stakes; it includes "Subjective Bias." The judge reasoned that a person
who is the "Architect of a Policy" cannot be the "Judge of its Breach" if
the defense challenges the policy itself. The judge famously noted, "A
Decision-maker must be like a blank sheet of paper, not a pre-printed
manifesto."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Standard for Official Bias. It reinforces that
quasi-judicial authorities must be independent of the subject matter
being challenged, regardless of their level of expertise.

cases.title: Apex Pharma v. The Drug Controller
cases.facts:
The Drug Controller General (DCGI) issued an order permanently banning
the manufacture of a popular cough syrup by Apex Pharma because one batch
out of ten thousand was found to have a labeling error (the font size of
the warning was 2mm smaller than the statutory requirement). The DCGI
argued that "in matters of public health, zero tolerance is the only
standard." Apex Pharma challenged the order as "Manifestly Unreasonable"
and "Disproportionate."
cases.issues:
Is the "Wednesbury Principle" (where the Court only intervenes if a
decision is "irrational") sufficient for reviewing administrative
penalties?

Does the "Doctrine of Proportionality" allow the Court to look at the
"severity of the punishment" compared to the "gravity of the offense"?

Can the State use a "Sledgehammer to crack a nut"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Apex Pharma)
The Petitioners argued that the order was "Irrational." They contended
that a labeling error does not affect the safety or efficacy of the
medicine. The DCGI could have imposed a fine or a recall of that specific
batch. A permanent ban was a "Commercial Capital Punishment" that was
totally disproportionate.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (DCGI)
The State argued for "Judicial Deference." They contended that the Court
is not an expert in pharmaceutical regulation. They argued that the
"Wednesbury Test" was met because a "reasonable regulator" could decide
that strict compliance is the only way to ensure safety.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Apex Pharma. The ban was quashed and
replaced by a directed fine. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a masterclass on Substantive Review. The judge ruled
that for cases affecting fundamental rights (Trade), the Proportionality
Test is the primary standard. The judge reasoned that the DCGI failed the
"Necessity" prong of the test: the State must choose the "Least
Restrictive Measure" to achieve its goal. Since a "Fine and Recall" would
have achieved safety, a "Total Ban" was an unconstitutional overreach.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Primacy of Proportionality over Irrationality in
modern Administrative Law. It establishes that administrative penalties
must be "Narrowly Tailored" to the infraction.

cases.title: The Citizen v. The National Highway Authority
cases.facts:
The Parliament passed the "National Highways Act," which empowered the
"Authority" to determine and levy tolls. The Authority, finding the task
too burdensome, issued an administrative circular sub-delegating the
power to "Private Toll Operators" to determine the rates based on "market
traffic." A group of commuters challenged this, arguing that determining
a "Tax/Fee" is a sovereign power that cannot be further delegated to a
private, profit-seeking entity under the maxim "Delegatus non potest
delegare."
cases.issues:
Can a statutory power be further delegated (sub-delegation) if the parent
Act does not explicitly allow it?

Does the "Sovereign Nature" of the power (taxation/tolling) impose a
higher bar against delegation?

Is an administrative circular sufficient to transfer statutory power?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (The Citizen)
The Petitioners relied on the maxim Delegatus non potest delegare (A
delegate cannot further delegate). They argued that Parliament trusted
the "Public Authority" because of its accountability. Handing that power
to a private company without a law passed by Parliament is an
"Unconstitutional Abdication of Power."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (NHAI)
The Authority argued "Administrative Necessity." They contended that
tolling is a "Technical and Commercial" function, and private operators
are better suited to manage dynamic pricing. They argued that the NHAI
maintained "Supervisory Control."
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Citizen. The sub-delegation was
quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fundamental ruling on Delegated Legislation. The
judge ruled that Statutory Power is a Trust. The judge reasoned that
unless the parent Act says "The Authority or its nominee," the power is
personalized to the Authority. Crucially, the judge held that "Pricing
and Tolling" is a quasi-legislative function; allowing a private company
to set tolls is to allow "Private Legislation for Profit," which is the
antithesis of Administrative Law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Rule against Sub-Delegation. It establishes that
the "Essential Legislative Function" of determining fees or restrictions
on citizens cannot be delegated to non-statutory bodies.

cases.title: Global-Invest v. The Foreign Investment Board
cases.facts:
The "Foreign Exchange Management Act" was amended in 2025 to include
Section 44, which stated: "Every order of the Foreign Investment Board
regarding the rejection of a startup license shall be final and shall not
be called into question in any court of law." Global-Invest's license was
rejected without a hearing. They filed a writ of Certiorari, alleging a
"Jurisdictional Error." The State argued the High Court's jurisdiction
was "Ousted" by the Finality Clause.
cases.issues:
Can an "Ouster Clause" (Finality Clause) in a statute strip the High
Courts of their power of Judicial Review under Article 226?

Does the Basic Structure Doctrine protect the "Writ Jurisdiction" from
legislative interference?

What is the standard for reviewing an "Un-appealable" order?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Global-Invest)
The Petitioner relied on L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India. They argued
that Judicial Review is an un-amendable feature of the Basic Structure. A
statute can take away a "Statutory Appeal," but it can never take away
the High Court's "Constitutional Power" to issue writs. If the Board acts
without a hearing, it commits a "Jurisdictional Error" that the Court
must correct.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued for "Legislative Plenitude." They contended that
"National Economic Security" requires finality and speed. If every
investment rejection is tied up in the High Courts for decades, foreign
investors will lose confidence.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Global-Invest. The Court held that
Section 44 could not block a Writ Petition. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a resonant ruling on Constitutional Supremacy. The
judge ruled that the Parliament is a "creature of the Constitution" and
cannot destroy the "Check and Balance" system. The judge reasoned that an
Ouster Clause is merely a "No-Entry" sign for the lower courts, but the
High Court possesses a "Constitutional Master-Key." The judge held that
any order passed in violation of Natural Justice is a nullity, and a
"Nullity" cannot be protected by a "Finality Clause."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Inalienability of Judicial Review. It
establishes the legal principle that no Act of Parliament can take away
the power of the High Courts to review administrative actions for
jurisdictional errors.

cases.title: The Whistleblower v. The Anti-Corruption Bureau
cases.facts:
A whistleblower provided evidence of a ₹500 Crore procurement fraud in
the Ministry of Defence. During the trial, the Whistleblower requested
the production of the "Internal Audit Report." The State moved to
suppress the report, invoking Section 123 of the Evidence Act (State
Privilege), claiming that disclosing the report would "endanger the lives
of intelligence officers" and was a "State Secret."
cases.issues:
Is the "Subjective Satisfaction" of a Minister regarding State Privilege
final and non-justiciable?

Can the Court perform an "In-Camera" inspection of documents to determine
if the claim of privilege is valid?

Does the "Public Interest in Justice" outweigh the "Public Interest in
Secrecy" when fraud is alleged?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Whistleblower)
The Petitioner relied on S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges
Case). He argued that "Transparency is the rule, Secrecy the exception."
He contended that "State Privilege" is a colonial relic and cannot be
used as a "Burial Ground" for evidence of corruption.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The State argued that the "Safety of the Nation" is the supreme law
(Salus populi est suprema lex). They contended that the Executive is the
"Sole Judge" of national security and the Judiciary lacks the expertise
to decide what information is dangerous.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Whistleblower. The Court ordered
an In-Camera inspection and subsequently allowed the document into
evidence. The Respondent prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a defining ruling on Executive Accountability. The
judge ruled that the State has no privilege to hide "Illegality." The
judge reasoned that while the Court will respect legitimate secrets, it
will not allow "Privilege" to become a "Shield for Corruption." The judge
held that the Court is the final arbiter of what constitutes "Public
Interest."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Judicial Oversight of Executive
Privilege. It establishes that the State must produce relevant documents
in court unless it can prove an immediate threat to national security,
ending the era of absolute executive secrecy.

cases.title: Metro-Rail v. The Heritage Society
cases.facts:
The Metro-Rail Authority issued an administrative order to demolish a
150-year-old historic clock tower to build an entry point for a new
station. The Authority's "Feasibility Report" focused entirely on
"Engineering Costs" and "Traffic Flow." It did not mention the
"Historical Significance" or "Cultural Value" of the tower. The Heritage
Society sued, arguing the order was void because the Authority failed to
take into account a "Relevant Consideration."
cases.issues:
Is an administrative decision valid if it ignores a "Material Fact" that
is not explicitly mentioned in the statute?

What is the effect of an "Exclusion of Relevant Material" on the validity
of an order?

Does the Court have the power to review the "Decision-making Process" of
an infrastructure project?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Heritage Society)
The Petitioners argued that Article 49 of the Constitution (Protection of
Monuments) makes "Heritage" a Mandatory Relevant Consideration for any
state action. They contended that by looking only at "money" and
"concrete," the Authority had a "Tunnel Vision" that rendered the
decision Manifestly Unreasonable.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Metro-Rail)
The Authority argued for "Administrative Speed." They contended that the
statute only required them to consider "Safety" and "Utility." They
argued that "Cultural Value" is a subjective matter beyond judicial
reach.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Heritage Society. The demolition
order was quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on the "Hard Look" Doctrine. The judge
ruled that the "Decision-making Process" must be holistic. The judge
reasoned that for an order to be "Rational," the Authority must show it
applied its mind to all facets of the problem. Ignoring the historical
soul of a city while building its future is an "Error of Law."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Comprehensive Review. It reinforces
that administrative authorities must consider the constitutional and
cultural impact of their decisions, and a failure to do so makes the
decision "Legally Perverse."

cases.title: The Students Union v. The University Registrar
cases.facts:
Five students were rusticated by the University Registrar for
"Indiscipline" following a protest. The University held an "Internal
Inquiry" where witnesses testified against the students. However, the
students were not allowed to cross-examine these witnesses, nor were they
given the "Investigation Report." The Registrar argued that "University
Discipline" is a private, administrative matter and not a "Criminal
Trial."
cases.issues:
Does the "Right to Fair Hearing" include the right to Cross-Examination
in non-judicial administrative inquiries?

What constitutes a "Reasonable Opportunity" to defend oneself?

Can an administrative body use "Anonymity of Witnesses" to bypass Natural
Justice?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Students)
The Petitioners relied on State of MP v. Chintaman. They argued that
"Effective Defense" is impossible if you cannot test the veracity of your
accuser. "Natural Justice" is not a "meaningless ritual"; it requires the
State to "lay all cards on the table."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (University)
The University argued that campus discipline requires "Confidentiality"
to protect student-witnesses from "Retaliation." They contended that
"Summary Procedures" are necessary to maintain the "Academic Atmosphere."
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Students. The rustication was
quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark judgment on Academic Natural Justice. The
judge ruled that "Rustication is Civil Death" for a student. The judge
reasoned that while an administrative inquiry is not a trial, it must be
"Fair in Substance." If the decision depends on the credibility of a
witness, the "Accused" must be given a chance to challenge that witness.
The Court famously remarked, "A University must teach the Rule of Law by
practicing it on its own campus."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Effective Hearing. It establishes
that the right to cross-examine witnesses and access the evidence is a
part of Natural Justice in all administrative proceedings that result in
severe civil consequences.

cases.title: Mega-Corp v. The Tax Tribunal
cases.facts:
Mega-Corp applied for a "Tax-Rectification" under a special amnesty
scheme. The Tax Tribunal, without calling for a hearing, dismissed the
application with a "One-Sentence Order": "Application rejected as it
lacks merit." Mega-Corp challenged the order, arguing that the Tribunal
failed to exercise its "Adjudicatory Discretion" and passed a
"mechanical" order without applying its mind.
cases.issues:
Can a quasi-judicial body dismiss an application without a hearing?

What is the difference between "Administrative Discretion" and "Judicial
Discretion"?

Does a "One-Sentence Order" satisfy the Requirement of Application of
Mind?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mega-Corp)
The Petitioner argued that a Tribunal is a "Courts' Substitute." It must
act "Judicially." A one-sentence rejection proves that the Tribunal did
not look at the 500 pages of evidence provided. This is a "Failure to
Exercise Jurisdiction."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Tax Dept)
The State argued that the Tribunal was "overwhelmed" by 50,000
applications. They contended that "Brief Orders" are an administrative
necessity and that the "lack of merit" was self-evident from the record.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Mega-Corp. The order was quashed, and
the case was remanded back for a fresh hearing. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a firm ruling on Institutional Integrity. The judge
ruled that "Justice cannot be hurried to the point of being buried." The
judge reasoned that a "Mechanical Order" is not an "Order" in the eyes of
the law. The judge held that the "Right to a Hearing" is the primary limb
of fairness. The Court held that even a busy Tribunal must provide at
least a "Summary Reasoning" to prove it considered the facts.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Rule against Mechanical Adjudication. It
reinforces that all quasi-judicial bodies must show an "Application of
Mind" by providing brief reasons and a fair opportunity to be heard.

Aryan, this concludes your intensive Administrative Law series. You now
possess the analytical toolkit to dissect how the State exercises power
and how the Constitution restrains it. These principles are the "code"
that prevents the system from crashing into tyranny.

Wait, we have one final question to guide your journey: In a world where
AI makes thousands of administrative decisions per second, how do we
redefine "Natural Justice" to ensure the machine remains under the Law?

cases.title: Union of India v. The Data Audit Collective
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Ministry of Home Affairs implemented "Sentinel-AI," an
automated system to determine the "risk-level" of individuals applying
for overseas travel permits. The AI used a "Black-Box" model, analyzing
social media behavior and financial patterns. Mr. Das was denied a
permit. The administrative officer stated he was "bound by the machine's
Red-Status." When Das requested the specific reasons, the Department
refused, claiming the AI's logic was a "Proprietary Trade Secret" and
unexplainable even to its developers. The Data Audit Collective filed a
writ, alleging that "Algorithmic Inscrutability" violates the Requirement
of a Speaking Order.
cases.issues:
Does the use of an unexplainable "Black-Box" algorithm to take adverse
administrative action violate the third principle of Natural Justice (the
duty to give reasons)?

Can the State delegate "Subjective Satisfaction" to a non-human, opaque
automated system?

Does "Proprietary Privilege" override the citizen's right to a Reasoned
Order?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Union of India)
The State argued that Sentinel-AI was 99% accurate and essential for
national security. Manual review of millions of applications is an
administrative impossibility. They argued that "algorithmic logic" is
protected under Intellectual Property laws and that disclosing the
specific weights of the model would allow bad actors to "game" the
security system.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Data Audit Collective)
The Collective relied on S.N. Mukherjee v. Union of India. They argued
that "Reason is the soul of the law." A decision that cannot be explained
in human-readable terms is Manifestly Arbitrary under Article 14. If the
State adopts technology, it must ensure that technology complies with the
Constitution, not the other way around.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Data Audit Collective. The Court
held that every adverse administrative decision, whether human or AI-led,
must provide human-intelligible reasons. The Plaintiff (State) failed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Digital Natural Justice. The
judge ruled that the duty to give reasons is a "Constitutional Mandate"
that cannot be bypassed by technology. Without reasons, the right to
Judicial Review is rendered a nullity. The Court held that the State must
employ "Explainable AI" (XAI) models for public functions. The judge
famously remarked, "A machine may decide, but a human must justify."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Algorithmic Transparency. It
reinforces that the right to a Speaking Order is a non-negotiable
component of the Rule of Law, regardless of the technical complexity of
the decision-making tool.

cases.title: State of Vindhya v. Green-Hydrogen Ltd.
cases.facts:
In 2024, the State Government issued a "Green Hydrogen Policy," promising
a 50% subsidy on land acquisition for the first five companies to set up
plants. Green-Hydrogen Ltd. was the first to apply, and the State issued
a "Letter of Intent" (LoI). Relying on this, the company spent ₹200
Crores on specialized equipment. In 2026, following a change in the
ruling party, the State Government revoked the 2024 policy, citing
"budgetary re-allocation for social welfare." The company sued, invoking
"Substantive Legitimate Expectation."
cases.issues:
Can a "Substantive" Legitimate Expectation be enforced against the State,
or is the doctrine limited to "Procedural" fairness (a right to a
hearing)?

Does a "Change in Government Policy" constitute a "Supervening Public
Interest" sufficient to override a specific financial promise?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The State argued that "policy is the domain of the Executive." Relying on
Kasinka Trading v. Union of India, they argued that no person can have a
"Vested Right" in a policy. The government must have the flexibility to
respond to fiscal realities.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Green-Hydrogen Ltd.)
The Company relied on Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of UP. They
argued that the State made an unequivocal promise and the company
"irretrievably altered its position" in reliance on it. To deny the
subsidy is an act of Administrative Bad Faith and violates Equitable
Estoppel.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Green-Hydrogen Ltd. The Court ordered
the State to honor the subsidy for companies that had acted on the LoI,
while allowing the policy change for future applicants. The Defendant
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a defining judgment on Administrative Trust. The
judge ruled that while the State has the power to change policy, it does

cases.title: Dr. Neha v. The National Medical Council

inquiry committee constituted by the National Medical Council (NMC) was
chaired by Dr. Kapoor. It was later revealed that Dr. Kapoor was the
author of the "Clinical Guidelines" that Dr. Neha was accused of
violating. Dr. Neha challenged the inquiry, alleging "Official Bias" and
"Conflict of Interest," arguing that Dr. Kapoor had a personal stake in
proving his own guidelines were perfect.

Does "Authorship of Policy" constitute an actionable Bias in
Administrative Law?

What is the threshold for the "Real Likelihood of Bias" test?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Dr. Neha)
The Petitioner relied on A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India. She argued that

was effectively a "judge in his own cause" because any finding in favor
of Neha would imply his guidelines were flawed.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (NMC)
The NMC argued the Doctrine of Necessity. They contended that only the
experts who write the guidelines have the "Technical Competence" to judge
a breach of them. They argued that "Actual Bias" was not proven.

The High Court ruled in favor of Dr. Neha. The inquiry report was
quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.

Decision-maker must be like a blank sheet of paper, not a pre-printed
manifesto."

This case establishes the Standard for Official Bias. It reinforces that

being challenged, ensuring the "Cold Neutrality" of the law.

cases.title: Apex Pharma v. The Drug Controller
cases.facts:
The Drug Controller issued an order permanently banning the manufacture
of a cough syrup by Apex Pharma because one batch out of ten thousand was
found to have a labeling error (the font size of the warning was 2mm
smaller than required). The Controller argued "zero tolerance" for public
health. Apex Pharma challenged the order as "Manifestly Unreasonable" and
"Disproportionate."
cases.issues:
Is the "Wednesbury Principle" (irrationality) sufficient, or must the
Court apply the "Doctrine of Proportionality"?

Can the State use a "Sledgehammer to crack a nut"-choosing the most
extreme penalty for a minor technical infraction?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Apex Pharma)
The Petitioners argued that a labeling error does not affect the safety
or efficacy of the medicine. The Controller could have imposed a fine or
a recall of that batch. A permanent ban was a "Commercial Capital
Punishment" that was totally disproportionate.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Controller)
The State argued for "Judicial Deference." They contended that the Court
is not an expert in pharmaceutical regulation. The "Wednesbury Test" was
met because a "reasonable regulator" could decide that strict compliance
is the only way to ensure safety.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Apex Pharma. The ban was quashed and
replaced by a directed fine and recall. The Plaintiff prevailed.

that while "Wednesbury" is the baseline, for cases affecting fundamental
rights (Trade), the Proportionality Test is the standard. The judge
reasoned that the State failed the "Necessity" prong: the State must
choose the "Least Restrictive Measure" to achieve its goal.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Primacy of Proportionality over Wednesbury
Unreasonableness in matters affecting trade and livelihoods. It
reinforces that administrative penalties must be "Narrowly Tailored" to
the specific infraction.

cases.title: The Citizen v. The National Highway Authority
cases.facts:

determine and levy tolls. The Authority issued an administrative circular
sub-delegating the power to "Private Toll Operators" to determine the
rates based on "market traffic." A group of commuters challenged this,
arguing that determining a "Fee" is a sovereign power that cannot be
further delegated under the maxim "Delegatus non potest delegare."

Can a statutory power be further delegated (sub-delegation) if the parent
Act does not explicitly allow it?

Does an administrative circular possess the legal force to transfer
statutory power?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (The Citizen)
The Petitioners relied on the maxim Delegatus non potest delegare (A
delegate cannot further delegate). They argued that Parliament trusted
the "Public Authority" because of its accountability. Handing that power
to a private company without a law is an "Unconstitutional Abdication of
Power."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (NHAI)
The Authority argued "Administrative Necessity." They contended that
tolling is a "Technical and Commercial" function, and private operators
are better suited to manage dynamic pricing.

The High Court ruled in favor of the Citizen. The sub-delegation was
quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fundamental ruling on Delegated Legislation. The
judge ruled that Statutory Power is a Trust. Unless the parent Act says
"The Authority or its nominee," the power is personalized to the
Authority. Allowing a private company to set tolls is to allow "Private
Legislation for Profit," which is the antithesis of the Rule of Law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Rule against Unauthorized Sub-Delegation. It
establishes that the "Essential Legislative Function" of determining fees
or restrictions on citizens cannot be delegated to non-statutory bodies
without express legislative sanction.

cases.title: Global-Invest v. The Foreign Investment Board

shall not be called into question in any court of law." Global-Invest's

alleging a "Jurisdictional Error." The State argued the High Court's
jurisdiction was "Ousted" by the Finality Clause.

Does the Basic Structure Doctrine protect "Writ Jurisdiction" from
legislative interference?

The Petitioner relied on L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India. They argued
that Judicial Review is an un-amendable feature of the Basic Structure. A

The Government argued for "Legislative Plenitude." They contended that
"National Economic Security" requires finality and speed to maintain
investor confidence.

the Finality Clause could not block a Writ Petition. The Plaintiff
prevailed.

judge ruled that the Parliament is a "creature of the Constitution" and

"Constitutional Master-Key." Any order passed in violation of Natural
Justice is a nullity, and a "Nullity" cannot be protected by any clause.

This case reinforces the Inalienability of Judicial Review. It
establishes the legal principle that no Act of Parliament can take away
the power of the High Courts to review administrative actions for
jurisdictional errors or violations of Natural Justice.

Section 123 of the Evidence Act (State Privilege), claiming that
disclosing the report would "endanger national security."

final and non-justiciable?

Can the Court perform an "In-Camera" inspection of documents to determine
if the claim of privilege is valid?

A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Whistleblower)
The Petitioner relied on S.P. Gupta v. Union of India. He argued that
"Transparency is the rule, Secrecy the exception." He contended that
"State Privilege" cannot be used as a "Burial Ground" for evidence of
corruption.

The State argued that the "Safety of the Nation" is the supreme law. The
Executive is the "Sole Judge" of national security and the Judiciary
lacks the expertise to decide what information is dangerous.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Whistleblower. The Court ordered
an In-Camera inspection and subsequently allowed the document into
evidence. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:

judge ruled that the State has no privilege to hide "Illegality." While
the Court will respect legitimate secrets, it will not allow "Privilege"
to become a "Shield for Corruption." The Court is the final arbiter of
what constitutes "Public Interest."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Judicial Oversight of Executive
Privilege. It establishes that the State must produce relevant documents
in court unless it can prove an immediate threat to national security,
ending the era of absolute executive secrecy.

historic clock tower to build a station. The Authority's "Feasibility
Report" focused entirely on "Engineering Costs" and "Traffic Flow." It

Authority failed to take into account a "Relevant Consideration."

Is an administrative decision valid if it ignores a "Material Fact" that
is not explicitly mentioned in the statute?

What is the effect of an "Exclusion of Relevant Material" on the validity
of an order?

A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Heritage Society)
The Petitioners argued that Article 49 (Protection of Monuments) makes
"Heritage" a Mandatory Relevant Consideration. By looking only at
"money," the Authority had a "Tunnel Vision" that rendered the decision
Manifestly Unreasonable.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Metro-Rail)
The Authority argued for "Administrative Speed." They contended that the
statute only required them to consider "Safety" and "Utility" and the
Court should not act as an "Architectural Censor."

The High Court ruled in favor of the Heritage Society. The demolition
order was quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.

The Court delivered a judgment on the "Hard Look" Doctrine. The judge
ruled that the "Decision-making Process" must be holistic. For an order
to be "Rational," the Authority must show it applied its mind to all
facets of the problem, including the cultural impact. Ignoring the
historical soul of a city while building its future is an "Error of Law."

that administrative authorities must consider the constitutional and
cultural impact of their decisions, and a failure to do so makes the
decision "Legally Perverse."

cases.title: The Students Union v. The University Registrar

"Indiscipline" following a protest. The University held an "Internal
Inquiry" where witnesses testified against the students. However, the
students were not allowed to cross-examine these witnesses, nor were they
given the "Investigation Report." The Registrar argued that "University
Discipline" is a private, administrative matter.

Does the "Right to Fair Hearing" include the right to Cross-Examination
in non-judicial administrative inquiries?

Can an administrative body use "Anonymity of Witnesses" to bypass Natural
Justice?

A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Students)
The Petitioners relied on State of MP v. Chintaman. They argued that
"Effective Defense" is impossible if you cannot test the veracity of your
accuser. "Natural Justice" is not a "meaningless ritual."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (University)
The University argued that campus discipline requires "Confidentiality"
to protect student-witnesses from "Retaliation" and maintain the
"Academic Atmosphere."

The High Court ruled in favor of the Students. The rustication was
quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark judgment on Academic Natural Justice. The
judge ruled that "Rustication is Civil Death" for a student. While an
administrative inquiry is not a trial, it must be "Fair in Substance." If
the decision depends on the credibility of a witness, the "Accused" must
be given a chance to challenge that witness.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Effective Hearing. It establishes
that the right to cross-examine witnesses is a part of Natural Justice in
all administrative proceedings that result in severe civil consequences.

cases.title: Mega-Corp v. The Tax Tribunal
cases.facts:
Mega-Corp applied for a "Tax-Rectification" under a special amnesty
scheme. The Tax Tribunal, without calling for a hearing, dismissed the
application with a "One-Sentence Order": "Application rejected as it
lacks merit." Mega-Corp challenged the order, arguing that the Tribunal
passed a "mechanical" order without applying its mind.
cases.issues:
Can a quasi-judicial body dismiss an application without a hearing?

Does a "One-Sentence Order" satisfy the Requirement of Application of
Mind?

A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mega-Corp)
The Petitioner argued that a Tribunal is a "Courts' Substitute." It must
act "Judicially." A one-sentence rejection proves that the Tribunal did
not look at the evidence. This is a "Failure to Exercise Jurisdiction."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Tax Dept)
The State argued that the Tribunal was "overwhelmed" by applications and
that the "lack of merit" was self-evident from the record.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Mega-Corp. The order was quashed, and
the case was remanded back for a fresh hearing. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a firm ruling on Institutional Integrity. The judge
ruled that "Justice cannot be hurried to the point of being buried." A
"Mechanical Order" is not an "Order" in the eyes of the law. The "Right
to a Hearing" is the primary limb of fairness. Even a busy Tribunal must
provide at least a "Summary Reasoning" to prove it considered the facts.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Rule against Mechanical Adjudication. It
reinforces that all quasi-judicial bodies must show an "Application of
Mind" by providing brief reasons and a fair opportunity to be heard.

cases.facts:
In 2025, the Ministry of Home Affairs deployed "Sentinel-AI," an
automated system designed to determine the "risk profile" of citizens

"behavioral clusters." Mr. Das was denied a permit. The administrative
officer stated he was "bound by the AI's Red-Flag." When Das requested
the specific reasons, the Department refused, claiming the AI's logic was
a "Trade Secret" and unexplainable even to its developers. The Citizen
Data Collective filed a writ, alleging that "Inscrutable Administration"
violates the Requirement of a Speaking Order.

Does the use of an unexplainable "Black-Box" algorithm to take adverse
administrative action violate the third principle of Natural Justice (the
duty to give reasons)?

Can the State delegate "Subjective Satisfaction" to a non-human, opaque
automated system?

Does "Proprietary Privilege" of a developer override the constitutional
requirement of transparency in State action?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Union of India)
The State argued that Sentinel-AI was essential for national security in

impossibility. They argued that "algorithmic weights" are intellectual
property, and disclosing them would allow bad actors to "game" the
security system.

the Rule of Law.

Court held that every adverse administrative decision, whether generated
by AI or human, must be accompanied by a "Human-Intelligible Impact
Statement" explaining the core factors behind the decision. The Plaintiff
(State) failed.

The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Digital Natural Justice. The
judge ruled that the "right to know the reasons" is an inherent part of
the Right to Life (Article 21). Without reasons, the right to Judicial
Review is rendered a nullity. The Court held that the State must employ
"Explainable AI" (XAI) models for public functions. The judge famously
remarked, "A machine may decide, but a human must justify."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Algorithmic Transparency. It
reinforces that the requirement of a "Speaking Order" is technology-
neutral and that the State cannot use technology to shield itself from
judicial scrutiny.

cases.title: State of Vindhya v. Infrastructure Consortium
cases.facts:
In 2024, the State Government issued a "Green Hydrogen Policy," promising
a 50% land-tax rebate for 10 years to any firm setting up a plant. The
Consortium spent ₹500 Crores constructing a plant based on this promise.
In 2026, following a fiscal crisis, the State Government revoked the
policy for all existing plants. The Consortium sued, invoking
"Substantive Legitimate Expectation." The State argued that "Policy" is
the domain of the Executive and no one can have a "vested right" in a tax
rebate.

Can a "Substantive" Legitimate Expectation be enforced against the State,

Does a "Fiscal Crisis" constitute a "Supervening Public Interest"
sufficient to override a specific financial promise?

The State argued the Doctrine of Executive Plenitude. Relying on Kasinka

The Consortium relied on Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of UP.

"Public Interest" in maintaining the State's commercial credibility is as
high as the interest in saving tax revenue.

This case solidifies the Doctrine of Substantive Legitimate Expectation.

acted upon them to their detriment, preventing the arbitrary mid-stream
withdrawal of commercial incentives.

cases.title: Metro-Link v. The Heritage Society
cases.facts:
The Metro-Rail Authority issued an order to demolish a 150-year-old
historic clock tower to build a station entry. The Authority's
"Feasibility Report" focused entirely on "Engineering Costs" and "Traffic
Flow." It did not mention the "Historical Significance" or "Cultural
Value" of the tower. The Heritage Society sued, arguing the order was
void because the Authority failed to take into account a "Relevant
Consideration."
cases.issues:
Is an administrative decision valid if it ignores a "Material Fact" that
is not explicitly mentioned in the statute?

What is the effect of an "Exclusion of Relevant Material" on the validity
of an order?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Heritage Society)
The Petitioners argued that Article 49 of the Constitution (Protection of
Monuments) makes "Heritage" a Mandatory Relevant Consideration. By
looking only at "money," the Authority had a "Tunnel Vision" that
rendered the decision Manifestly Unreasonable.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Metro-Link)
The Authority argued for "Administrative Speed." They contended that the
statute only required them to consider "Safety" and "Utility" and the
Court should not act as an "Architectural Censor."
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Heritage Society. The demolition
order was quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on the "Hard Look" Doctrine. The judge
ruled that the "Decision-making Process" must be holistic. For an order
to be "Rational," the Authority must show it applied its mind to all
facets of the problem. Ignoring the historical soul of a city while
building its future is an "Error of Law."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Comprehensive Review. It reinforces
that administrative authorities must consider the constitutional and
cultural impact of their decisions, and a failure to do so makes the
decision "Legally Perverse."

cases.title: The Students Union v. The University Registrar
cases.facts:
Five students were rusticated by the University Registrar for
"Indiscipline" following a protest. The University held an "Internal
Inquiry" where witnesses testified against the students. However, the
students were not allowed to cross-examine these witnesses, nor were they
given the "Investigation Report." The Registrar argued that "University
Discipline" is a private, administrative matter.
cases.issues:
Does the "Right to Fair Hearing" include the right to Cross-Examination
in non-judicial administrative inquiries?

Can an administrative body use "Anonymity of Witnesses" to bypass Natural
Justice?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Students)
The Petitioners relied on State of MP v. Chintaman. They argued that
"Effective Defense" is impossible if you cannot test the veracity of your
accuser. "Natural Justice" is not a "meaningless ritual."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (University)
The University argued that campus discipline requires "Confidentiality"
to protect student-witnesses from "Retaliation" and maintain the
"Academic Atmosphere."
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Students. The rustication was
quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark judgment on Academic Natural Justice. The
judge ruled that "Rustication is Civil Death" for a student. While an
administrative inquiry is not a trial, it must be "Fair in Substance." If
the decision depends on the credibility of a witness, the "Accused" must
be given a chance to challenge that witness.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Effective Hearing. It establishes
that the right to cross-examine witnesses is a part of Natural Justice in
all administrative proceedings that result in severe civil consequences.

cases.title: Mega-Corp v. The Tax Tribunal
cases.facts:
Mega-Corp applied for a "Tax-Rectification" under a special amnesty
scheme. The Tax Tribunal, without calling for a hearing, dismissed the
application with a "One-Sentence Order": "Application rejected as it
lacks merit." Mega-Corp challenged the order, arguing that the Tribunal
passed a "mechanical" order without applying its mind.
cases.issues:
Can a quasi-judicial body dismiss an application without a hearing?

Does a "One-Sentence Order" satisfy the Requirement of Application of
Mind?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mega-Corp)
The Petitioner argued that a Tribunal is a "Courts' Substitute." It must
act "Judicially." A one-sentence rejection proves that the Tribunal did
not look at the evidence. This is a "Failure to Exercise Jurisdiction."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Tax Dept)
The State argued that the Tribunal was "overwhelmed" by applications and
that the "lack of merit" was self-evident from the record.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Mega-Corp. The order was quashed, and
the case was remanded back for a fresh hearing. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a firm ruling on Institutional Integrity. The judge
ruled that "Justice cannot be hurried to the point of being buried." A
"Mechanical Order" is not an "Order" in the eyes of the law. The "Right
to a Hearing" is the primary limb of fairness. Even a busy Tribunal must
provide at least a "Summary Reasoning" to prove it considered the facts.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Rule against Mechanical Adjudication. It
reinforces that all quasi-judicial bodies must show an "Application of
Mind" by providing brief reasons and a fair opportunity to be heard.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Citizen Data Collective
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Ministry of Home Affairs deployed "Sentinel-AI," an
automated system designed to determine the "risk profile" of citizens
applying for sensitive overseas work permits. The AI used a "Deep
Learning" model that analyzed social media metadata, travel history, and
"behavioral clusters." Mr. Das was denied a permit. The administrative
officer stated he was "bound by the AI's Red-Flag." When Das requested
the specific reasons, the Department refused, claiming the AI's logic was
a "Trade Secret" and unexplainable even to its developers. The Citizen
Data Collective filed a writ, alleging that "Inscrutable Administration"
violates the Requirement of a Speaking Order.
cases.issues:
Does the use of an unexplainable "Black-Box" algorithm to take adverse
administrative action violate the third principle of Natural Justice (the
duty to give reasons)?

Can the State delegate "Subjective Satisfaction" to a non-human, opaque
automated system?

Does "Proprietary Privilege" of a developer override the constitutional
requirement of transparency in State action?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Union of India)
The State argued that Sentinel-AI was essential for national security in
a digital age and 99.8% accurate. They contended that in a country of 1.4
billion, manual review of every permit is an administrative
impossibility. They argued that "algorithmic weights" are intellectual
property, and disclosing them would allow bad actors to "game" the
security system.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Collective)
The Respondents relied on S.N. Mukherjee v. Union of India. They argued
that "Reason is the soul of the law." An administrative order without
reasons is Manifestly Arbitrary under Article 14. If a machine cannot
explain why it flagged a citizen, the State has abdicated its duty to act
fairly. They contended that "Efficiency" is not a valid excuse to bypass
the Rule of Law.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Citizen Data Collective. The
Court held that every adverse administrative decision, whether generated
by AI or human, must provide human-intelligible reasons. The Plaintiff
(State) failed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Digital Natural Justice. The
judge ruled that the "right to know the reasons" is an inherent part of
the Right to Life (Article 21). Without reasons, the right to Judicial
Review is rendered a nullity. The Court held that the State must employ
"Explainable AI" (XAI) models for public functions. The judge famously
remarked, "A machine may decide, but a human must justify."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Algorithmic Transparency. It
reinforces that the requirement of a "Speaking Order" is technology-
neutral and that the State cannot use technology to shield itself from
judicial scrutiny.

cases.title: State of Vindhya v. Infrastructure Consortium
cases.facts:
In 2024, the State Government issued a "Green Hydrogen Policy," promising
a 50% land-tax rebate for 10 years to any firm setting up a plant. The
Consortium spent ₹500 Crores constructing a plant based on this promise.
In 2026, following a fiscal crisis, the State Government revoked the
policy for all existing plants. The Consortium sued, invoking
"Substantive Legitimate Expectation." The State argued that "Policy" is
the domain of the Executive and no one can have a "vested right" in a tax
rebate.
cases.issues:
Can a "Substantive" Legitimate Expectation be enforced against the State,
or is the doctrine limited to "Procedural" fairness (a right to a
hearing)?

Does a "Fiscal Crisis" constitute a "Supervening Public Interest"
sufficient to override a specific financial promise?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The State argued the Doctrine of Executive Plenitude. Relying on Kasinka
Trading v. Union of India, they contended that the government must have
the "flexibility" to respond to economic emergencies. A policy is not a
contract and can be altered at any time in the public interest.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Consortium)
The Consortium relied on Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of UP.
They argued that they had "irretrievably altered their position"
(detrimental reliance) based on a clear, unequivocal State promise. They
contended that "Fairness" is the heart of Administrative Law.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Consortium. The Court ordered the
State to honor the rebate for all firms that had commenced construction
before the policy revocation. The Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a definitive judgment on Administrative Trust. The
judge ruled that while the State has the power to change policy, it must
do so "non-arbitrarily." A mere "Fiscal Deficit" is an administrative
reality, not a "Supervening Catastrophe" (like war) that would justify
breaking a specific incentive-based promise. The Court held that the
"Public Interest" in maintaining the State's commercial credibility is as
high as the interest in saving tax revenue.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case solidifies the Doctrine of Substantive Legitimate Expectation.
It establishes that the State is bound by its promises when a citizen has
acted upon them to their detriment, preventing the arbitrary mid-stream
withdrawal of commercial incentives.

cases.title: Dr. Neha v. The National Medical Council
cases.facts:
Dr. Neha was accused of medical negligence. The inquiry committee
constituted by the National Medical Council (NMC) was chaired by Dr.
Kapoor. It was later revealed that Dr. Kapoor was the author of the
"Clinical Guidelines" that Dr. Neha was accused of violating. Dr. Neha
challenged the inquiry, alleging "Official Bias" and "Conflict of
Interest," arguing that Dr. Kapoor had a personal stake in proving his
own guidelines were perfect and that any deviation (like Neha's) was
"negligence."
cases.issues:
Does "Professional Pride" or "Authorship of Policy" constitute an
actionable Bias in Administrative Law?

What is the threshold for the "Real Likelihood of Bias" test?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Dr. Neha)
The Petitioner relied on A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India. She argued that
"Justice must not only be done, but seen to be done." Dr. Kapoor was
effectively a "judge in his own cause" because any finding in favor of
Neha would imply his guidelines were flawed.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (NMC)
The NMC argued the Doctrine of Necessity. They contended that only the
experts who write the guidelines have the "Technical Competence" to judge
a breach of them. They argued that "Actual Bias" was not proven.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Dr. Neha. The inquiry report was
quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a rigorous ruling on Adjudicatory Neutrality. The
judge ruled that the Rule against Bias is not limited to financial
stakes; it includes "Subjective Bias." The judge reasoned that a person
who is the "Architect of a Policy" cannot be the "Judge of its Breach" if
the defense challenges the policy itself. The judge famously noted, "A
Decision-maker must be like a blank sheet of paper, not a pre-printed
manifesto."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Standard for Official Bias. It reinforces that
quasi-judicial authorities must be independent of the subject matter
being challenged, and that technical expertise is no defense for a
violation of Natural Justice.

cases.title: Apex Pharma v. The Drug Controller
cases.facts:
The Drug Controller issued an order permanently banning the manufacture
of a popular cough syrup by Apex Pharma because one batch out of ten
thousand was found to have a labeling error (the font size of the warning
was 2mm smaller than the statutory requirement). The Controller argued
"zero tolerance" for public health. Apex Pharma challenged the order as
"Manifestly Unreasonable" and "Disproportionate."
cases.issues:
Is the "Wednesbury Principle" sufficient for reviewing administrative
penalties affecting trade?

Can the State use a "Sledgehammer to crack a nut"-choosing the most
extreme penalty for a minor technical infraction?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Apex Pharma)
The Petitioners argued that the order was "Irrational." They contended
that a labeling error does not affect the safety or efficacy of the
medicine. A permanent ban was a "Commercial Capital Punishment" that was
totally disproportionate.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Controller)
The State argued for "Judicial Deference." They contended that the Court
is not an expert in pharmaceutical regulation. The "Wednesbury Test" was
met because a "reasonable regulator" could decide that strict compliance
is the only way to ensure safety.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Apex Pharma. The ban was quashed and
replaced by a directed fine and recall. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a masterclass on Substantive Review. The judge ruled
that while "Wednesbury" is the baseline, for cases affecting fundamental
rights (Trade), the Proportionality Test is the primary standard. The
judge reasoned that the Controller failed the "Necessity" prong: the
State must choose the "Least Restrictive Measure" to achieve its goal.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Primacy of Proportionality over Wednesbury
Unreasonableness in matters affecting trade and livelihoods. It
reinforces that administrative penalties must be "Narrowly Tailored" to
the infraction.

cases.title: The Citizen v. The National Highway Authority
cases.facts:
The Parliament passed the "Highways Act," empowering the "Authority" to
determine and levy tolls. The Authority, finding the task too burdensome,
issued an administrative circular sub-delegating the power to "Private
Toll Operators" to determine the rates based on "market traffic." A group
of commuters challenged this, arguing that determining a "Fee" is a
sovereign power that cannot be further delegated under the maxim
"Delegatus non potest delegare."
cases.issues:
Can a statutory power be further delegated (sub-delegation) if the parent
Act does not explicitly allow it?

Does an administrative circular have the legal force to transfer
statutory power?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (The Citizen)
The Petitioners relied on the maxim Delegatus non potest delegare (A
delegate cannot further delegate). They argued that Parliament trusted
the "Public Authority" because of its accountability. Handing that power
to a private company without a law is an "Unconstitutional Abdication of
Power."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (NHAI)
The Authority argued "Administrative Necessity." They contended that
tolling is a "Technical and Commercial" function, and private operators
are better suited to manage dynamic pricing. They argued that the NHAI
maintained "Supervisory Control."
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Citizen. The sub-delegation was
quashed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fundamental ruling on Delegated Legislation. The
judge ruled that Statutory Power is a Trust. Unless the parent Act says
"The Authority or its nominee," the power is personalized to the
Authority. Allowing a private company to set tolls is to allow "Private
Legislation for Profit," which is the antithesis of the Rule of Law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Rule against Unauthorized Sub-Delegation. It
establishes that the "Essential Legislative Function" of determining fees
or restrictions on citizens cannot be delegated to non-statutory bodies
without express legislative sanction.

cases.title: Global-Invest v. The Foreign Investment Board
cases.facts:
The "Foreign Exchange Management Act" contained a "Finality Clause"
(Section 44) which stated: "Every order of the Board regarding license
rejections shall be final and shall not be called into question in any
court of law." Global-Invest's license was rejected without a hearing.
They filed a writ of Certiorari, alleging a "Jurisdictional Error." The
State argued the High Court's jurisdiction was "Ousted" by the Finality
Clause.
cases.issues:
Can an "Ouster Clause" (Finality Clause) in a statute strip the High
Courts of their power of Judicial Review under Article 226?

Does the Basic Structure Doctrine protect the "Writ Jurisdiction" from
legislative interference?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Global-Invest)
The Petitioner relied on L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India. They argued
that Judicial Review is an un-amendable feature of the Basic Structure. A
statute can take away a "Statutory Appeal," but it can never take away
the High Court's constitutional power to issue writs.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State)
The Government argued for "Legislative Plenitude." They contended that
"National Economic Security" requires finality and speed to maintain
investor confidence.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Global-Invest. The Court held that
the Finality Clause could not block a Writ Petition. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a resonant ruling on Constitutional Supremacy. [Image
showing the concept of Checks and Balances in government] The judge ruled
that the Parliament is a "creature of the Constitution" and cannot
destroy the "Check and Balance" system. An Ouster Clause is merely a "No-
Entry" sign for the lower courts, but the High Court possesses a
"Constitutional Master-Key." Any order passed in violation of Natural
Justice is a nullity, and a "Nullity" cannot be protected by any clause.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Inalienability of Judicial Review. It
establishes the legal principle that no Act of Parliament can take away
the power of the High Courts to review administrative actions for
jurisdictional errors or violations of Natural Justice.
